Introduction This guidance note will take you through steps to consider your data sharing needs, whether a data sharing agreement is right for you and what to include.
This guide was originally developed in partnership with CABI and GODAN.
It draws on the experiences of those organisations in participating in data sharing agreements for agronomy programmes.
While the guide has been written to be more generally applicable, we welcome feedback on the content from those working in other contexts to help us improve it.
Please leave a comment on the document or email policy@theodi.org with your thoughts.
What is a data sharing agreement?
A data sharing agreement is an agreement between two or more organisations about how to share data.
It will define what data is being shared and for how long, and any restrictions on its use.
Data sharing agreements can take many forms, depending on the scale and complexity of the data sharing.
For example memoranda of understanding, service level agreements and formal legal contracts could all be data sharing agreements.
A data sharing agreement is a set of common rules binding for all the organisations involved in a data sharing initiative.
The agreement should be drafted in clear, concise language that is easily understood.
Data sharing needs Is the data already available?
If the data is already published then a sharing agreement may not be needed.
Users who want to use the data should be able to access it from where it has been published (such as a website or portal), and use it according to the conditions of its existing licence.
If these conditions are too restrictive, or the data needs to include more attributes, question 2 will help you to consider whether a data sharing agreement is appropriate.
Do I need a data sharing agreement?
Data can be shared in lots of ways and it is important to consider which option suits you best and whether a data sharing agreement is appropriate.
The following scenarios will help you consider what is right for your circumstances.
Scenario A: the data is published but the licence is too restrictive for the data to be used in this circumstance.
For example the current licence may prohibit commercial use.
Consider whether you can alter the way the published data is licensed to reduce restrictions and move along The Data Spectrum towards open.
Scenario B: the data is not yet published and you want to pass it to another organisation for them to use with no charge or restrictions.
Consider publishing the data as open data for anyone to access, use or share.
Scenario C: the data is not already published and is not appropriate to publish it openly (e.g. to protect privacy, or because it is commercially sensitive, or for other legal reasons).
A data sharing agreement to share directly between organisations may be best in this instance.
Scenario D: the data is not already published and contains data from a third party organisation(s), which could restrict how widely it can be shared.
A data sharing agreement – including addressing any third party intellectual property rights – may be most appropriate in this instance.
Am I able to share this data?
Before proceeding with drafting a data sharing agreement, or publishing data under an open licence, you should consider whether you have the appropriate rights and permissions.
You may have previously collected data for other purposes.
Data protection legislation, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) might place restrictions on whether you are able to publish and reuse that data in other contexts.
Regardless of legislation, there may be ethical considerations that should inform whether you can publish and share data.
Tools like the data ethics canvas can support you in exploring these issues.
You may need to take steps to anonymise or aggregate data, or gain consent from the people who may be impacted by a data release before proceeding.
What a good data sharing agreement should include The sections below suggest some key areas to include in your data sharing agreement.
They are not exhaustive but should help you decide on its contents.
aim is to be clear about what, when and how data will be supplied, what it can be used for and who is responsible for maintaining it.
Context This section sets out reasons for sharing data and the parties involved.
Consider including: a description of the entities signing the agreement a statement summarising the purpose of the agreement- eg what are the objectives of the programme, and objectives of data sharing the main contacts in each organisation for queries about the data – eg the data asset owner any financial agreement, that may cover how both costs and benefits are distributed The data This section focuses on describing the data itself, so it is clear what will be shared specifically.
Consider: What data will be shared?
○ Specify the name, description and any unique reference number to identify the data.
■ NB: if the data is described in an inventory or catalogue accessible to both parties, it might be described most easily and clearly by referencing its catalogue entry.
○ What is the structure (e.g. attributes, parameters, etc) of the data that will be shared?
○ What time period does the data cover (if appropriate)?
○ Across what geography and at what spatial resolution (if appropriate)?
○ What format is the data in?
○ What quality does the data need to be?
Can this be specified and measured?
○ What is the source of the data?
■ Is it from one organisation or from a combination of different sources (intellectual property rights could have implications for how the data can be shared and used) ■ Do the contributing sources know that the data will be shared and are you committing them to providing regular updates through this agreement?
Is this a one-off transfer or will updates be made?
If updates are required: ○ would they be as necessary corrections to the data?
○ would they be as additions to the data?
○ how regularly can they be made?
If this is a one-off transfer of data, then when will the data be provided?
Roles and responsibilities.
Where possible, include: ○ name and contact details of organisation representatives ○ description of role and responsibilities- eg who will prepare and update data, who will monitor implementation of the agreement, who to contact to resolve disputes etc
Sharing This section focuses on how the data will get from one party to another.
Consider: How is the data going to be shared between different parties?
Where can the data be accessed or transferred?
Are there any potential cross-border issues that could affect access, such as geographic location?
Where is the data going to be stored?
Who is responsible for hosting the data?
Is the transfer method secure?
(This is particularly important if personal, sensitive or national security data is being shared) Examples of how data can be shared, supplied and hosted include: open access publication depositing them with a specialist data centre, data archive or data bank making them available online via a project or institution website making them available via a secure, online interface that provides limited access to data making them available at a secure physical location depositing them in an institutional repository submitting them to a journal to supplement a publication making them available informally between researchers on a peer-to-peer basis How long is the data going to be shared for?
If sharing is for a fixed time period, must the recipient destroy their copies of the data at the end of the agreement?
○ How will this be verified?
Are there local or international laws that could affect the data being shared?
Use This section focuses on specifying what the data can be used for.
This can be linked to the data’s source.
Where data comes from more than one source (ie different organisations) you will need to check with the original data providers whether you have the right to share the data, and confirm any restrictions on use.
Consider: What permissions have been granted to each party that describe how they can use the data?
What requirements do they need to follow in order to retain those permissions, e.g. to attribute the source of the data What restrictions might limit the use of the data.
For example ○ Can the recipient share the data with other parties?
■ If so, under what conditions?
■ Can the data be sold?
○ Can the data be used in commercial products and services?
Consider whether you need permissions (e.g from third parties or individual consent) to share or use the data If you are using a template data licence, then which licence are you using?
Derived data This section focuses on products that might be produced that incorporate data that has been shared.
Consider: Who will have rights over, or have access to what has been produced using the data that has been shared?
Can derived data be published and, if so, what licensing restrictions might apply to how that data is published for reuse by others Are there any requirements from the funding donor for products being produced using the data?
For example, the donor may have an open access policy which obliges the recipient of funding to make outputs available within a specific timeframe eg 6 months after completion of grant.
See for example the Gates Foundation open access policy .
Handling personal data If the data to be shared includes personal data, you must include clauses to specify how the data will be secured, in transit to third parties and while in their control the retention period for the data limitations to third-party use of the data You must ensure that data being shared with the intended recipient is covered in an agreement made with the people that the data is about, along with how it is collected, processed and used.
If the personal data includes data about EU citizens then there should be clauses to specify compliance with the GDPR.
Other local or international laws may also affect how personal data can be shared, and these should also be checked.
You should be transparent about how you are sharing personal data with others, e.g.
by publishing who you are sharing data with, how that data is being shared, etc. We recommend adopting these principles for organisations handling personal data to help build trust and transparency around how you share data.
What to do once you have shared the data Agreeing to share the data is the first step.
Once you’ve agreed what, when and how to share data, it is important to put a plan in place to manage the data supply.
This should be part of the overall data management plan.
Important things to consider and plan for are: Keep a record of the data you share and who you share it with (ie in an inventory) Scheduling and resourcing updates
Quality checking: is a certain quality required?
How will you be confident you are providing data that is suitably accurate?
Seeking feedback from the data user/recipient on its quality, completeness, format, timeliness etc Ensuring that the data user/recipient is complying with the terms of your agreement Resourcing any changes to how the data is managed based on user feedback Informing the data users/recipients about any planned changes to the scope, provision or availability of the data in future Additional resources Data sharing agreement guide ​ from Chatham House Data sharing agreement template and support pack ​ from CGIAR Outputs management plans ​ from Welcome foundation Data sharing checklist ​ from the UK Information Commissioner Data Sharing Code of Practice ​ from the UK Information Commissioner Data licences: ○ Creative Commons ○ Open Government Licence ​ from the UK ○ Other ​ non-open licences ​ from the UK Licensing guidance: ○ What are the impacts of non open licences from the ODI ○ Reusers guide to open data licences from the ODI ○ Publishers guide to open data licences from the ODI

About this checklist and resources: This checklist provides a step-by-step guide and tools to help lawtech startups and scaleups work with data holders, like a corporation or a law firm, to access data.
It is designed to support direct, mutually beneficial data sharing between a lawtech and a data holder, which enables the lawtech to access data to train a model and/or improve their product and, in turn, such a product helps a data holder solve a specific problem or realise a market opportunity, with an additional scenario where a data holder shares data to benefit society, consumers, or their sector as a whole, from which the data holder might gain an indirect and non-immediate benefit.
For lawtechs participating in the Lawtech Sandbox, Lawtech UK can help facilitate the process, for example by identifying data holders, educating a data holder about the benefits of open innovation and data sharing, making introductions, or providing guidance, and regardless of who is supporting, it is for the lawtech to lead the activities at each step of the checklist.
Create a data wishlist.
Understand the potential data holder’s needs and how to sell.
Identify who you need to speak to within the data holder organisation.
Assess and mitigate any legal, ethical and business risks associated with data sharing.
Understand the data holder’s business priorities and challenges and how you can help.
Who can act as your internal champion?
Investigate what data is available.
Set objectives and a timeline.
Agree commitments from each side.
Before an introduction to a data holder.
These steps will help you define your value proposition and help structure any conversation you have with a data holder.
Create a data wishlist.
List all the types of data you would like to access, and list it per sector and/or type of organisation or
category you need to build your solution.
You can use this template.
Be as specific as you can to make it easier for a data holder to respond to your request.
Understand the potential data holder’s needs and how to sell.
Which organisations are likely to hold the data on your data wishlist, what challenges do they face, and how could you persuade them to release data to you?
Some of the most convincing approaches are: a.
Data insights: does the data holder need insights from its or its clients’ data?
Resource and overhead reduction.
Does the data holder lack the internal resource and/or skills to utilise their data?
Could you help them reduce their overheads by, for example, structuring their data?
Client need.
If you’re approaching a law firm, can your solution help them better serve their own clients’ needs?
Increased efficiency.
Can your solution improve internal operations for the data holder, and what is the measurable value?
Reputational benefits.
Could a partnership lead to positive press coverage for the data holder from either an innovation or pro bono angle?
Identify who you need to speak to within the data holder organisation.
The key is to understand who is the custodian of the data, who makes the decisions, and who can champion your solution internally.
At a law firm, it might be the Head of Innovation, CIO or CTO, or a partner in charge of the practice area related to your data request; at a large corporation, it will likely be the General Counsel or a Legal Operations lead.
Do your research, ask for help from industry contacts, make enquiries directly.
To help you identify who you need to talk to, consider: a.
Who are the people most affected by the problem you’re trying to solve?
Do they have an existing process for working with lawtechs or vendors and for sharing data?
Who is already using the data, internally and externally, and how are they using it?
Assess and mitigate any legal, ethical and business risks associated with data sharing.
Anticipate what risks (perceived or otherwise) the data holder associates with sharing data and prepare a mitigation strategy.
Common concerns include: confidentiality, legal privilege, reputational risk, losing a competitive advantage, and understanding who “owns” the data.
To help you address these concerns, consider: a.
What data will you get access to, and for how long?
How will you use and take care of it?
Will the data be anonymised or pseudonymised?
How will you access the data?
Where can you work on it?
Who owns the intellectual property rights in the outcome of a data sharing process?
What will you offer in return for access to the data—for example, free access to your product for a certain length of time?
Existing relevant codes, frameworks and principles, such as the Information Commissioner’s Data Sharing Code of Practice, the Solicitors Regulation Authority code of conduct, and Microsoft’s AI principles; now you’ve identified a list of organisations and individuals you’d like to approach and have a strategy for that.
If you’re part of a programme like the Lawtech Sandbox, then you’ll have access to warm introductions with data holders already interested in open innovation and data sharing.
If you don’t have access to a direct introduction, Step 3 should help you to identify who within the company you should reach out to.
You will need to be clear, persistent and bold.
In the first conversation.
During this stage, spend time diving deeper into a data holder’s challenges, explore what data they hold, and identify who can act as an internal champion for your request and/or product.
Understand the data holder’s business priorities and challenges and how you can help.
Lead with the data holder’s challenges, rather than selling your solution or the data access request, do your homework up front, and use the meetings to dive deeper and test your assumptions about how your solution or proposed pilot meets those challenges, and explore: a.
What might their motivation to share data be?
Are they looking to reduce costs, increase efficiencies, generate better outcomes for clients or do more pro bono work?
What, if any, concerns do they have around data sharing?
Is it general risk aversion, a lack of knowledge on data sharing, or something specific?
Are there blockers that can’t be resolved in a timeframe that works for you?
If there isn’t a potential mutual benefit, be prepared to move on quickly, as data holders in the legal sector can be hesitant to disclose what challenges they face or to share data, so it is worth going where the energy is.
Who can act as your internal champion?
Multiple people may need to be involved in the decision to share data, at a legal, technical and strategic level.
An internal champion can help you navigate internal teams and requirements, and help you communicate your solution’s potential value in a way that is tailored to the data holder.
At a law firm, an innovation manager or passionate practitioner could help guide your proposal through any investment committee and/or get it approved.
In a corporation, it might be the legal operations lead, general counsel or an advocate in the department relevant to the product, e.g., customer services, finance or sales.
Investigate what data is available.
An organisation may not have a clear picture about what data they hold, where it’s held, what data processing resources are required, or what they can legally share.
You can explore this with them and suggest an approach.
The data holder also might be able to suggest data you hadn’t thought of.
You may find it valuable to request a data sample, so you can identify potential issues and gain a better understanding of what resources are required to process the data.
Once the data holder is engaged.
Once a data holder has, in principle, agreed to share data and work together, these are the steps to consider when you’re negotiating the partnership and access to data.
Set objectives and a timeline.
Set attainable, scheduled and measurable objectives.
Be flexible, as data in large organisations is often scattered across different internal systems and departments, or managed by a third-party vendor, and it may take time for them to gather the required data for sharing if there is not an established process in place.
Consider the following when setting objectives.
What are the assumptions and expectations for the data sharing?
Is this a proof of concept, pilot or a partnership?
How confident are you both that you will be able to achieve the desired outcomes—do you need to be agile and iterative or do you both have a clear idea about the result you are going to achieve?
Can you support the data holder to prepare the data or reduce their overheads in other ways?
Agree commitments from each side.
Follow up with an email setting out the key terms to your agreement to share data.
It is sensible to put in place a formal agreement, and it is likely that the data source will require this before any data is shared.
Any agreement should cover both the legal and technical aspects of sharing data.
You can use this template agreement here, which has been developed by Lawtech UK in collaboration with the ODI.
Finally, be prepared to source and speak to multiple data holders and to others who may help you connect with them.
As you do, learn as you go, and continue to revisit the steps to iterate what you’re offering and asking for.

Data Sharing Agreement/Document Checklist and Guidance for GPs and Practices Londonwide LMCs is aware of the increasing complexity and number of information and Data Sharing Agreements and documents (DSAs) which practices are receiving to review and sign.
Whilst Londonwide LMCs cannot endorse, support or approve any information sharing or DSAs/documents, we have put together this checklist and guidance to help GPs and practices in reviewing the agreements they receive in order to be able to make an informed decision on whether to sign them or not.
If you are unfamiliar with what constitutes a DSA, please read through the guidance section first and then use the checklist.
Please note this checklist does not constitute legal advice and is guidance only.
There may be other considerations/processes and documents that you may have to take into account or have in place to fully comply with all the requirements of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) (Regulation (EU) 2016/679)/Data Protection Act 2018 (DPA and other data protection legislation.
You should liaise with your Data Protection Officer (DPO) and/or the CCG provided DPO and DPO support service, and other parties to the DSA, including taking legal advice where appropriate to ensure that you are compliant with GDPR/DPA 2018 and other data protection legislation.
This checklist has been produced with advice from LMC Law Ltd and Protecture.
Checklist for GPs and Practices reviewing a Data Sharing Agreement (DSA)/Document Review the DSA using the questions provided in the checklist below.
The checklist is divided into three parts: essential information, necessary information, and your role.
For each question, record the answer.
If the answer is ‘partly’ or ‘no’, request clarification from the owner of the agreement.
Keep a record of the information provided, if the DSA itself has not been amended to include it.

Contain a list of the categories of personal data which will be shared in the dataset, including any ‘special category’ data and any de-identified data?
Identify or describe the group of data subjects whose personal data will be shared and how they are expected to be identified?
Describe the objective(s) of the sharing, how the sharing supports and is necessary for those objectives?

This includes making clear which parties are the disseminators and recipients of which data sets – the relationship must be clearly defined.

Include a version number, details of the approval process and state how any variations to the agreement, including new signatories, will be handled?
Provide references to other documents such as contracts, over-arching protocols or standards which the DSA relies on?

If you have answered ‘partly’ or ‘no’ to any of the questions in the checklist, you may wish to seek clarification on these essential points before signing the agreement, or to decide whether the risk to your practice and patients is acceptable.
You must document this decision in your data protection records.
What to do next Once you have completed this checklist, if you are satisfied that the DSA is fit for purpose and that you can deliver your part in the sharing relationship without problems, and you want to sign it, then you should: Update your practice privacy notice with the privacy notice information provided for this DSA and ensure this is displayed/available for patients Update your practice data mapping with any additional data flows from the DSA and update your practice ROPA (Record of Processing Activities) Ensure all relevant practice staff are aware of the sharing if they are asked questions by patients.
Guidance What is a Data Sharing Agreement?
This is a catch-all term for documents which describe the arrangements where personal data is being transferred, copied or accessed between organisations.
A DSA can take different forms: it could be a separate document, it could be part of a suite or tier of documents, it may be a separate sharing agreement associated with a contract, or the data sharing terms may form part of a contract.
Whilst some organisations prefer to have legally-binding agreements to limit their liability, data sharing arrangements are not required to be legally-binding agreements, as long as all of the requirements of data protection and confidentiality law are met.
However, if an agreement is intended to create legal relations, then it is a ‘contract’ under English law, even if it is not described that way.
What’s the difference between a Data Sharing Agreement and a Data Processor Agreement?
A Data Processor Agreement is a legally-binding contract between a Data Controller and a Data Processor which sets out the instructions for processing and strict limits on what the Processor can do with the data.
For example, if a GP Practice as a Data Controller wishes to use a mailing house to write to its patients, then the mailing house would require access to personal data from the GP Practice in the form of patient names and address details.
The mailing house would be processing the data on behalf of the GP Practice and a data processing agreement or contract would be required, detailing the parties involved and the processing activity being undertaken.
This is a legislative requirement, as Data Processors can only process on instruction from a Data Controller.
A DSA is usually an operational document which describes one-way, two-way or multiple way distribution of personal data between two or more Data Controllers.
Why have a Data Sharing Agreement?
The purpose of a DSA is to set out the sharing relationship clearly and carefully, so that everyone involved understands how it should work and what their individual and joint responsibilities are with regard to the data.
To achieve this, the DSA should be written in plain language without the use of jargon or obscure legal terms; and it should clearly describe the why, what, who, where and how of the sharing relationship so that there is no ambiguity or confusion on these points.
Although there is no law that explicitly says a DSA must be put into place, the Accountability Principle of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) requires that reliable records are created for all data processing activities.
Therefore, having DSAs in place for data sharing relationships is a necessary part of demonstrating compliance with data protection law.
Do I have to sign this Data Sharing Agreement?
If your practice is party to a DSA which you don’t fully understand or don’t agree with you may be placing the practice and your patients at risk by proceeding.
To protect yourselves and your patients, you should always ask for clarification on any aspects within the agreement which are missing, inappropriate or not properly explained before you sign.
By signing the agreement, you are accepting a degree of responsibility (and possibly legal liability) for the data sharing relationship, so it is important to make sure you understand and can deliver your part.
How do I make sense of this Data Sharing Agreement document?
Ideally, a DSA should be easy to read, understand and interrogate.
However, this is not always the case, especially where the DSA forms part of a contract.
In its most basic form, a DSA should tell the reader the following: Why the sharing will happen: The purpose of the sharing activities and the lawful basis for each purpose or sharing activity The objectives of the sharing, and why the sharing of personal data is necessary to meet those objectives.
(It must demonstrate that this sharing activity is proportionate to the objectives, which could not be achieved otherwise) The power to share: the functions or powers of your organisation and any legal obligation to share.
What personal data is being shared: What categories of personal data are involved, and which of these are ‘special category’ personal data Which particular group or set of patients will be affected What you need to tell people about the data sharing and how you will communicate that information.
How the sharing works: The journeys that the data will take between/among the organisations The systems and processes for collecting, storing, sending/receiving and using the data The relationships between the organisations: whether they are independent Data Controllers (independently decide the why, what and how of processing) or Joint Data Controllers (jointly decide the why, what and how of processing) , and the boundaries of these relationships Which organisation is responsible overall for the sharing agreement Who in each organisation is accountable for making sure that the terms of the sharing agreement are met
Who needs to be informed about the terms of the sharing agreement How changes to the agreement or the relationships will be managed What arrangements need to be in place to provide individuals with access to their personal data if they request it Measures to ensure adequate security are in place to protect the data Agreed common retention periods for the data Processes to ensure that secure deletion takes place, where appropriate.
To be able to evaluate and understand the terms of a DSA, you will need to have an understanding of data protection and confidentiality law.
If you are not familiar with any of the following terms, you should brush up on your knowledge of the following before tackling the DSA: Data Subject Data Controller Data Processor Joint Data Controllers Data Protection Principles Subject Access Requests 3rd country/conditions for transfer Lawful basis of processing.
Why can’t Londonwide LMCs or my LMC review and approve the Data Sharing Agreement for my practice?
Londonwide LMCs cannot endorse, support or approve any information sharing or DSAs/documents, and we don’t have the resources or expertise to review each DSA/document in detail.
However, we do wish to ensure that commissioners/providers give assurance to practices that the key requirements are in place and in a format that is accessible and readable.
So, in addition to this checklist and guidance for GPs and practices, Londonwide LMCs has also developed, with legal assistance, an assurance checklist for commissioners/providers.
This will be provided to the organisation/author of the DSA and they will be asked to review the checklist against their proposed DSA and to sign that the DSA covers the items specified in the checklist and that the DSA meets current data protection requirements.
A copy of the completed assurance checklist for commissioners/providers, along with a copy of the Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) for the DSA, should accompany/or be made available to practices when the DSA is sent to them.
The DPIA will identify any risks that can’t be fully addressed and as part of the process these should be highlighted to practices. Introduction Welcome to your sharing journey To make informed decisions about safeguarding and achieve quality outcomes for children and families, we have to share information either internally or with our partner agencies who also have responsibilities for safeguarding and prevention.
It has been frequently recognised in local and national reviews of practice that failing to share information at critical times has costs lives or led to detrimental outcomes.
A fear of sharing sensitive information must not be a blocker to safeguarding and promoting the welfare of children and families at risk.
The relevant UK government departments and independent non-departmental government bodies responsible for protecting children and/or regulating data protection therefore set out policy, legislation and statutory guidance on how the child protection system should work and data protection compliance is achieved at the same time.
Those pieces of legislation are in place for local authorities and their sharing partners to be used to justify information sharing and to allow it in a safe and legal way.
Some legislation puts a duty on us to share and others provide us with power to do so.
What is safeguarding?
The Care Quality Commission (CQC) describes safeguarding as protecting people’s health, wellbeing and human rights, and enabling them to live free from harm, abuse and neglect.
It’s fundamental to high-quality health and social care.
The Department for Education defines safeguarding as follows within their ‘Working Together to Safeguard Children’ guide to inter-agency working to safeguard and promote the welfare of children: a.
Protecting children from maltreatment b.
Preventing impairment of children’s mental and physical health or development c.
Ensuring that children are growing up in circumstances consistent with the provision of safe and effective care d.
Taking action to enable all children to have the best outcomes Safeguarding must therefore be seen as a protection of wellbeing (including physical, mental & emotional); a prevention of harm and reduction of risk through care and support requiring information sharing.
This allows intervention in immediate situations demanding the safeguarding of children and individuals but also sharing for prevention and early intervention in less immediate or high-risk situations.
First steps to get started Our guidance and template have been designed to take you through this journey.
It not only provides a template but also guidance including examples of what is needed, technical advice and signposting to other key documents which can help you.
Here is a simple flow chart of what you will need to do to go from having concerns about sharing data to sharing data legally and securely with confidence.
Why is the information needed?
What is the purpose for sharing the relevant information, think about the purpose for individuals, your organisation and the wider public.
What information is needed?
Be specific and descriptive, consider how often it is required, refer to the data item template available under 5.
‘Information to be shared by partners’ within the guidance document.
What organisation can provide the information?
Have you explored if the information is available already, maybe in other parts of your organisation.
Have you spoken to a counterpart in the potential sharing organisation who can advise you on what information is available and how often.
Have you completed a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)?
Be aware that a DPIA is likely to be a legal requirement.
Complete it before you start processing any data.
Use the guidance document to learn more about the requirement to complete a DPIA.
How will it be transferred?
Consider your options and assess the risk of those.
Transfers must be safe and secure, consult with your technical teams for more complex digital solutions (e.g. data transfer system to system or via Secure File Transfer Protocol [SFTP]).
Where will it be held?
Consider your options and assess the risk of those.
Any information must be held safe and secure, consult with your technical teams for more complex digital solutions.
Are you sure the information is accurate and not misleading?
Take all reasonable steps to ensure the personal data you hold is not incorrect or misleading.
If you discover that personal data is incorrect or misleading you must take steps to correct or erase it as soon as possible.
Carefully consider any challenges to the accuracy of personal data.
How will you process it?
Define what solutions are available to process the information (e.g. data warehouse, modelling, risk scoring, manual usage to inform cases), work closely with the relevant teams (e.g. analytics, IT, ethics).
How long will you keep it?
Follow your internal retention policy and establish how long you actually need the information.
Include any potential outcome products and long term requirements to hold the data.
How will you delete the data?
Follow your internal records retention or data destruction policy to assure safe destruction of the information you hold.
Consider the method depending on your storage solution to allow for safety of destruction.
The UK GDPR sets out seven key principles which should lie at the heat of your approach to processing personal data: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency Purpose limitation Data minimisation Accuracy Storage limitation Integrity and confidentiality (security) Accountability Please visit the ICO website for more detail on the principles.
What is next Once you have answered the essential questions, established details, and maybe started to complete your Data Protection Impact Assessment you can start to think about completing the Safeguarding Data Sharing Agreement template.
We hope this introduction, the Data Sharing Agreement template and accompanying guidance give confidence in pursuing the important journey to sharing relevant safeguarding information and reduces the fear of the unknown.
You might want to start with the glossary, if you glance through it now, it will help you going through the template.
And don’t forget the help available inside (Caldicott Guardian, information governance (IG) colleagues, Data Protection Officer, colleagues with experience of information sharing) and outside (we have provided a page with relevant links to valuable information within the guidance document) your organisation.
This Data Sharing Agreement template should be read and used alongside the guidance document.
Each section of the DSA is accompanied by the relevant examples of completed DSAs, example scenarios and guidance for completing the template.
Data Protection Officer advice and templates for relevant appendices are also included.
This Data Sharing Agreement Template and Guidance has been developed to: Help agencies and organisations to gain confidence and understanding of sharing for safeguarding purposes through the spectrum of sharing scenarios considering: Sharing with individual or multiple sharing partners Different types of partners (e.g. police, education, housing) Information sharing of specific data items (e.g. name and relevant services open to) to mass data sharing for analytical and risk modelling purposes Simple exchanges of data to the use of complex data warehouses Sharing for immediate safeguarding needs or early intervention and prevention Assist agencies and organisations by providing complex, specialised information governance requirements in an easily accessible and understandable way tackling issues like: Lack of expertise and knowledge Under resourced IG teams and relevant professional subject matter experts General resource and available time to research data protection requirements
Clarify commonly held misconceptions, such as: Not being able (allowed) to share Needing consent to share Only being able to share with statutory bodies Provide a Safeguarding Data Sharing Agreement Template and a corresponding Guidance Document with the required help for all levels of staff involved with an Information Sharing Initiative, including front line practitioners receiving and making data requests, through to Data Protection Officers tasked with reviewing and assessing the relevant Information Governance documentation to assure lawful and safe sharing/processing of data.
The Template and Guidance will lead you through the relevant sections and considerations required to allow sharing and to complete the Safeguarding Data Sharing Agreement.
Alternatively if you already have such agreements, it can be used to quality assure existing approaches.
It will assist by going through the relevant steps of consideration: What information are you requesting to receive or share and what is the purpose for doing so?
What organisations are involved and what are their specific roles and responsibilities?
Is a Data Protection Impact Assessment required and has it been completed (since the sharing is about children it is very likely that a DPIA will be required)?
Is the sharing justified (agree this in principle first) and what are your lawful bases and gateways that support the sharing?
How should you share the information (is it secure), what is happening to the data at every stage?
How will access to the information be limited to only those who need to have access?
How will you comply with transparency/informing obligations?
What quality checks are required to ensure the shared data is accurate and up-to-date?
What retention periods are appropriate?
How is destruction managed?
Purpose and benefits How to complete This section describes your sharing project/initiative and clearly sets out the purpose(s) for which the information is being shared.
This should be set out in clear and understandable language, describing the: nature (what is planned to be done with the personal data) scope (what does the processing cover – define the agreed scope of sharing set out in the agreement and outline how the data shared will be managed [i.e.
ensuring those that need it can see it, but those that don’t, can’t]) context (wider picture which might affect expectations or impact) purposes for processing (reason why personal data will be processed, benefit that the sharing will provide and/ or risks and possible consequences of not sharing and how sharing information is necessary to achieve those aims).
In these circumstances, ‘necessity’ with regard to justifying why information is shared should be in the context of ‘reasonably necessary’, rather than strictly or absolutely necessary.
Sharing has to be a proportionate response to the risk situation.
This section should set out what form the sharing agreement is covering, such as formalised sharing via a Multi-Agency Safeguarding Hub or in support of more ad hoc sharing via the inter-agency communications that take place around managing the welfare and safeguarding of children, or both.
The section also links to a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA), often required in support of data sharing and ideally performed early in the establishment of the sharing initiative.
Detail from the DPIA around purpose may also be drawn into this section.
The purpose section of the sharing agreement is the key section to be written by the relevant service leads at each organisation.
All partners/parties must agree on the purpose.
This section can use text/language from other documents, such as a business case, grant application or committee report.
This helps to ensure consistency.
You should include a short description of any statutory functions and/or applicable legislation, such as, “The Children Act 1989 requires all local authorities to...”.
You can also include a time period for the sharing, if the sharing relates to a project with an end date, or whether the sharing is expected to be ongoing.
Is this a pilot?
Is the project grant funded and are there any requirements or restrictions related to the funding?
Is there a plan to expand the project to new organisations or a larger number of data subjects if the pilot is successful?
What outcome do you expect the sharing to achieve?
Use plain English and spell out any abbreviations.
The purpose should be understandable to data subjects and the public in general.
Think about all possible benefits whether they are quantitative or qualitative.
Describe what benefits there will be to data subjects/individuals, the partner organisations, and society.
If using statements such as ‘to improve the welfare of children’, make sure you describe how the sharing will support that aim.
Consider including the potential consequences of not sharing, such as “serious case reviews have directly attributed the lack of good information sharing to subsequent death”.
Purpose and benefits – completed example Describe your sharing initiative/project (summary): To assess the risk to a child and make an informed decision on how to protect them and their family around concerns received within the Multi-Agency Safeguarding Hub (MASH) the MASH gathers information from partner agencies, children and their families.
Agencies within the MASH include, but are not limited to; the police, health, social care, early help, probation and schools.
Information is being gathered by sharing existing documentation and/or speaking to the parents, professionals working with the child and family or in some cases speaking with the child.
The MASH will record (date and time enquiry has been received, all information both sensitive and non-sensitive shared by partners, how it has been shared) what information has been shared and what has been retained after a decision has been made.
This will be facilitated by the lead social worker within the local authority.
Sharing rules are documented within the MASH Terms of Reference.
Sharing will commence through discussions, email exchange and access directly to systems (if available).
Please refer to the MASH DPIA V3 for further details.
Please also refer to the MASH police and non-police process chart in appendix 4 for further details.
The core benefit of the sharing arrangement is to ensure more timely and effective safeguarding services, increasing the prevention of adverse impacts on individuals and reducing the need for reactive services.
Clearly set out your purpose(s) and benefits for sharing (include a description of the nature, scope and context): Research and experience has demonstrated the importance of information sharing across professional boundaries to safeguard the welfare of children.
The Children Act 2004 emphasises the importance of safeguarding children by stating that relevant partner agencies which include the police, local authority children services and NHS Trusts – must make sure that functions are discharged with the aim of safeguarding and promoting the welfare of children.
The Act also states that they must promote cooperation between relevant partner agencies to improve the wellbeing of children in their area.
Information necessary for safeguarding decisions in relation to children and young people is held by numerous statutory and nonstatutory agencies.
Many sad cases across the UK have highlighted deficiencies within safeguarding partnerships in relation to the sharing of information and communication.
Some serious case reviews and inquiries (such as the Laming, Bichard and Baby P inquiries) have directly attributed the lack of good information sharing and communication to the subsequent death of an individual.
To deliver the best safeguarding decisions that ensure timely, necessary and proportionate interventions, decision makers need the full information picture concerning an individual and their circumstances to be available to them.
Information viewed alone or in silos may not give the full picture or identify the true risk.
All the information from various agencies needs to be available and accessible in one place; to keep children safe and assist signatories to this Agreement in discharging their obligations under the Act and other legislation.
Clearly set out your purpose(s) and benefits for sharing (include a description of the nature, scope and context): Purposes: identify, protect and support children early and effective identification of risk mitigation of risk to miss individuals (slipping through the safeguarding net) better understanding risks joint decision making and coordinated action stopping abuse/suffering before it occurs informed decision making on how to best ensure children are protected Who benefits: individuals (children, parents, families) organisations society
Purpose and benefits – example scenarios Scenario 1: A local authority and mental health trust seek to improve steps to prevent suicides by sharing personal data concerning individuals considered to be at risk of suicide.
The police are also asked and agree to provide relevant information but will not be accessing information routinely (though may request or be informed of relevant information on an ad-hoc basis).
The local authority and mental health trust have developed an application available to care professionals they employ in jointly provided suicide prevention services to manage information they need.
They have identified a number of risk factors in their individual data sources that are known to be related to suicide and by combining risk factors from both organisations will have a fuller picture of risks to individuals.
The application will also help them identify individuals who may be new to one service, but already known to the other.
The information sharing is necessary so that the staff involved with the individuals have the full picture of current risks, concerns and services involved with them, so can assess any change in circumstances and provide advice, guidance and support as required to prevent the risk of suicide and in time manage the care of the individual to the point when they no longer need the prevention service support.
They have documented this in a Data Sharing Agreement.
Scenario 2: The Local Authorities Early Years Portage and Inclusion Team provide support to families and early years practitioners for children from birth to five years, who have a disability and/or have special educational needs (SEN).
In order to provide the service needed, information sharing between the local authority, the child’s setting and other professionals who work with the child (e.g. GP, speech therapist, SEN Team) takes place.
The information sharing is necessary to complete and review educational progress over time and for planning the effective delivery of the service.
The information will be used to fulfil the duties placed on local authorities; namely for the provision and monitoring of support and services for families with young children, and planning future services and support, in the local area, and to ensure that awareness, and availability, so families can attend appropriate family support services.
They have documented this in a Data Sharing Agreement.
Purpose and benefits – What your DPO will need to know The purpose section is important for the DPO, to help them establish whether the sharing will follow the Data Protection Principles and be ‘fair and lawful’.
Review by the DPO is a good test of how well the purpose section has been set out and will help the DPO to identify gaps.
Further notes on what the DPO will want to know are included throughout this guidance.

Data Controller(s) / Joint Controller(s) How to complete It is essential to identify and document the roles of each organisation involved in any data sharing and determine if they are a controller, joint controller or processor (Processor(s) are covered in the next section under 4 Processor(s)) for the personal data being shared.
Data controllers decide why and how the personal data will be processed and shared.
We establish the status of each organisation to help determine the actions and risks for which each partner is responsible.
Some scenarios will be more straight forward than others.
Please use the help available on the following pages to establish the relevant roles and use 3E to document any joint controller arrangements (joint controllers must enter into an arrangement under Article 26 of the UK GDPR).
It may also be useful to identify if organisations identified as controllers contribute and/or view data (depending on the sharing scenario).
It is possible that some partners may only view data provided by others.
Such organisations might be controllers if they are determining the purposes and means of processing.
It is also possible that some organisations may be a controller, but not contribute or access any personal data.
Whilst this is uncommon, if they are involved in the determination of purposes and means, they are a controller.
An example may be an NHS Integrated Care Board (ICB) that has been involved in the development and governance of a Shared Care Record used by multiple health and social care organisations that it commissions to provide services.
Data Controller(s) / Joint Controller(s) – completed example Name of Organisation(s): Status: Police Controller Contributing data but no access to data contributed by sharing partners.
No access to data contributed by sharing partners.
Local Authority (LA) Joint-controller Use of data determined jointly by both LA & Mental Health Trust.
LA contributing data.
LA has additional processing responsibilities for processing of data contributed by Mental Health Trust and Police.
Access to all data contributed.
Mental Health Trust Joint-controller Use of data determined jointly by both LA & Mental Health Trust.
Mental Health Trust contributing data.
Access to all data contributed.
Voluntary sector commissioned provider Controller Not contributing data but accessing data provided by other partners to deliver commissioned service.
Has determined data that is available via this sharing is what it requires for it’s purposes.
Data controller(s) / joint controller(s) – example scenarios Scenario 1: Joint controller arrangement: Joint controller arrangement: A local authority and mental health trust seek to improve steps to prevent suicides by sharing personal data concerning individuals considered to be at risk of suicide.
The local authority and mental health trust have developed an application accessible over the internet to care professionals they employ in jointly provided suicide prevention services to manage information they need.
The Police are also asked and agree to share relevant information but do not require access to health and social care service information (though may request or be informed of relevant information on an ad-hoc basis).
The local authority and mental health trust are joint controllers of the data processed in the web application.
Scenario 2: Controller arrangement: Controller arrangement: A local authority, an acute NHS hospital trust and a community mental health NHS trust establish a regular multi-disciplinary team meeting to discuss a cohort of individuals that they either are all, or may all be involved with, providing complex care needs.
The meeting is to discuss both current caseload and potential individuals to come on to the caseload.
Each party brings notes to the meeting and shares what they think is relevant at the meeting.
No joint notes are taken and no shared systems are used.
Each party might record in their own notes some information from the others.
In this circumstance the organisations are likely to be separate controllers exchanging data as required as they do not have a shared asset (e.g. database) and whilst their objectives may be linked they are not necessarily the same.
Data controller(s) / joint controller(s) – What your DPO will need to know The DPO needs to know the relationships between all the parties to a data sharing agreement, so they can help establish each party’s responsibilities for complying with the Data Protection Principles.
Which organisations: have decided what data will be shared and how it will be handled (determination of purposes and means)?
will be contributing/sharing data?
will be accessing/receiving data?
will be handling/processing data on behalf of other organisations (acting as data processors)?
A Data Protection Impact Assessment is very likely to be required in many sharing scenarios and the DPO should be actively involved in advising on this at an early stage in the development.
Please also note that if a sharing initiative is a jointcontroller arrangement the Data Sharing Agreement (and all other relevant information governance documentation) must be completed jointly.

Data processor(s) – example scenarios Scenario 1: A local authority and mental health trust seek to improve steps to prevent suicides by sharing personal data concerning individuals considered to be at risk of suicide.
The police are also asked and agree to share relevant information but do not require access to health and social care service information (though may request or be informed of relevant information on an ad-hoc basis).
The joint controllers decide that they will instruct another organisation, an NHS commissioning support unit (CSU), to receive data feeds and display data in a system, that the CSU will maintain and support.
The CSU is therefore a data processor to the local authority and mental health trust as joint controllers.
They must have a contract/agreement in place as per Article 28 of the UK GDPR but can have a multi-party contract or either organisation can contract with the CSU, provided the other organisation is named as a beneficiary of the contract.
Scenario 2: A local authority is working with the police, public health nursing and the Department for Work and Pension (DWP) matching individuals data to households within a data warehouse to establish a single view of the child and family to enhance partnership working, early intervention and enable targeted support for children and their families.
The data warehouse is hosted by Microsoft Azure which must be classed as the data processor acting on behalf/instructions of the data controller.
A contract is in place as per legal requirement under UK GDPR, Article 28.
Data processor(s) – what your DPO will need to know This section must highlight clearly the Data Sharing Agreement personal data to be processed and by which organisation(s).
Consider processor due diligence; assurances that the processor will handle data appropriately (this may be included within a DPIA).
What agreement or other legal act is in place with the processor?
The DPO can assist in ensuring the agreement is compliant with UK GDPR article 28 requirements.
A Data Protection Impact Assessment is likely to be required for most safeguarding sharing.
This should identify data processors and must be reviewed and approved by the DPO before processing takes place.
Where there is a data processor, the DPO will need to see the agreement and check for appropriate clauses aligned to UK-GDPR article 28.
A data processor may be processing data on behalf of multiple controllers and each controller must have an appropriate Data Processing Agreement with the processor.
This can take the form of one contract with one controller as long as the other controllers are identified as ‘beneficiaries’ to that contract under the ‘Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999’.

Data shared between partners How to complete Service leads, operational staff and analytical staff who understand the information should work with the information governance team and the organisation’s DPO to decide what data/information is necessary and proportionate to share, to achieve the stated purpose.
The main considerations here are justification (why do we need this information and does the law allow us to process it for the intended purpose(s) and proportionality (how much information do we need and is there a way to reach the goal with less or pseudonymised or anonymised data).
For details about the different levels of identifiability please see Toolkit 2.
If your sharing initiative is straight-forward you will be able to list the required details directly in the data sharing agreement.
If the intended sharing of information is in a more informal way (corridor conversations) please see Toolkit 1 for further details.
Some (maybe less formal) sharing initiatives might require you to have a conversation to establish what information should be considered to be shared.
Partner organisations requesting data for safeguarding reasons do not necessarily understand what information is available to be shared.
Therefore it is important to push (what do you have that other parties are not asking for but in your view they need to know) and pull (what are the parties asking for) in order to get to the required results faster and safer.
It is good practice to include this in the Data Sharing Agreement to document good practice.
What is personal data?
Personal data relates to a directly or indirectly identified or identifiable living individual.
What identifies an individual could be as simple as a name or a number or could include other identifiers such as an IP address or a cookie identifier, or other factors.
If identifiers are being removed from data in order to pseudonymise the data it is still personal data under the UK GDPR.
Please see Toolkit 2 for more details around levels of identifiability.
What is special category data?
The UK GDPR singles out some types of data which are considered to be more sensitive and you may only process them in more limited circumstances.
Special category data includes: Racial or ethnic origin Political opinions Religious or philosophical beliefs Trade Union Membership Genetic data Biometric data Data concerning health Data concerning a person’s sex life Sexual orientation What is criminal offence data?
The UK GDPR gives extra protection to the personal data of offenders or suspected offenders.
This includes personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences or related security measures and covers information in the context of criminal activity, allegations, investigations and proceedings.
Please refer to 5F for a completed example of an indicator/ data index template.
If you have related sharing agreements already in place, check the data items listed in those and use those as a starting point for any new agreements as it is important to ensure consistency of language and terms.

Information shared between partners – example scenarios Scenario 1: The local Multi-Agency Safeguarding Hub (MASH) team makes assessments of risk to children and young people to allow informed decision making on what to do to best protect that child.
To make a decision the team share information between a number of partner agencies (e.g. police, health, social care, early help etc. ), children and families.
An overall Data Sharing Agreement is in place which helps all relevant partners to understand the purpose for the sharing, what will happen at each stage and what responsibilities they have.
The partners have now decided to put a specific Data Sharing Agreement in place to go into more details about responsibilities and security measures.
Because the MASH share different information depending on the case it has been decided to document overall likely types of data which can potentially be shared but to highlight that each practitioner within the MASH will need to make a balanced judgement on a case by case basis.
This will be with the formal structure of the MASH meetings, but also on an ad-hoc basis, either as a request/response or where deemed necessary a pro-active disclosure to reduce the risk of harm between relevant agencies.
Scenario 2: A local authority receives information from different partner organisations to better understand vulnerabilities of children, young people and their families within the relevant area.
The system/warehouse collating and matching the data allows the local authority to undertake analytical work to better understand how to improve or target the appropriate support to individuals or households.
The local authority is reviewing if it would be possible to share less data, but the proposed datasets offer the complete view of vulnerability based on the system.
Sharing less would mean the risk of failing to spot specific issues and potential further escalation of risk for individuals and families.
Failing to share personal data means opportunities for targeted support would be lost and the data immeasurably less valuable.
Data types and items have therefore been included to reduce this risk.
If going forward experience shows that some data items are not required the Data Sharing Agreement will be adjusted to reflect this and sharing of those items will be stopped.
It is notable the data protection principle related to what proportion of data to use starts with the words ‘adequate, relevant’ before mentioning ‘limited to...’
Information shared between partners – what your DPO will need to know The DPO needs to know what data will be shared, so they can help you identify which lawful basis conditions apply, and whether any of the personal data is likely to be processed for law enforcement purposes.
Different obligations apply when processing personal data for law enforcement purposes.
If you haven’t already completed a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA), listing the types of data will help the DPO decide if a DPIA is necessary.
Given the sensitivity and scale of the data shared for safeguarding and prevention purposes, it is likely that a DPIA will be required.
The DPO needs to know how you decided what data is necessary and proportionate to share, and who made that decision.
This helps the DPO decide if what you have listed is justifiable as necessary and proportionate and will help identify risks associated with the data sharing.
Think about what level of identity is required to fulfil the purpose of sharing the data.
Does the data need to be directly identifiable (linked to e.g. a name and address) or can it be pseudonymised (linked to a key e.g. ID number available to certain staff only) Please see Toolkit 2 for more details on anonymisation and options to reduce identifiability.

Lawfulness – UK GDPR lawful basis and Article 9 condition How to complete All personal data processing must comply with both the UK GDPR, and the Data Protection Act 2018 (DPA 2018).
If the purpose can be achieved without the processing of personal data (e.g. by processing anonymous data) you will not have a lawful basis to process.
To process personal data you must identify a lawful basis listed in the UK GDPR (Article 6).
The type of data, the purposes for processing, and the relationship with the individual (data subject) will impact which lawful basis is appropriate.
If you are processing special category personal data (listed in section 5 guidance) you must also meet a lawful basis condition in Article 9.
When processing special category data, you must also identify a condition from Schedule 1 Part 1, or Schedule 1 Part 2 of the DPA 2018 (see section 6a and guidance).
For processing personal data related to criminal convictions and offences (known as Law Enforcement processing) Article 10 of the UK GDPR applies, and a condition from the DPA 2018 Schedule 1 Part 3 must be identified.
For more detail please see Law Enforcement section on page 41.
Please use the lawful basis interactive guidance tool (refer to 6d) provided by the ICO and the help available on the following pages to assist you.
Identifying the appropriate lawful basis helps to meet Principle 1 of the GDPR, for fair and lawful processing of personal data.
The lawful basis affects how the rights of the data subject apply, and will determine how you meet your obligations to be transparent with a data subject about how their data is processed and shared.
For example, choosing 6(1)(c) for processing under a legal obligation, removes the right to erasure, to portability and to object.
An Appropriate Policy Document (APD) is required when using most of the public interest conditions under the DPA 2018.
If you are processing under Article 9(2)(g) for Safeguarding reasons it is very likely that you will require an APD (please see 6d if you require further details).
If you establish legitimate interests as your most appropriate basis in law you must complete a legitimate interests assessment to help you demonstrate compliance if required.
Please find details on this under 6d, Legitimate Interests.

Lawfulness – UK GDPR lawful basis and Article 9 condition – what your DPO will need to know Public authorities can only perform functions that they have ascribed to them in legislation and statute (see 6b for detail).
Such legislation provides the duty or power to deliver a service, but seldom do they reference data and information.
Therefore it can be difficult for staff to establish if the purpose of the intended sharing is specified in law or inferred (implied) by law and further more to establish the most appropriate lawful basis for processing under the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018.
It is important to assure that the specific purposes, context of processing and relationship to the individuals are considered in order to get it right from the start and that it is documented before processing commences.
If the purpose does not require the processing of the relevant data we do not have a lawful basis and consultation with the team is required to establish alternatives (e.g. using anonymised data, not sharing data).
It is also essential to assure accountability by documenting the lawful basis where necessary (Records of Processing Activities, Transparency Information, Data Sharing Agreement, DPIA etc. ).
Consider Schedule 1 of the DPA 18 for the processing of Criminal Offence Data.

Lawfulness – Data Protection Act 2018 How to complete If you are relying on UK GDPR Article 9 condition (b), (g), (h), (i), or (j) please make sure you also meet the relevant condition under Schedule 1, Parts 1 & 2 of the Data Protection Act 2018 (see under 6a – Lawfulness – Data Protection Act 2018 Your DPO will help you identify which schedule condition applies to the sharing).
The conditions under schedule 1 map to the GDPR article 9 conditions as follows: 9.2.b – employment, social security & social protection – DPA 2018, Schedule 1, Part 1, paragraph 1 9.2.g – substantial public interest – DPA 2018, Schedule 1, Part 2 (there are a number to choose from) 9.2.h – Provision of health and social care – DPA 2018, Schedule 1, Part 1, paragraph 2 9.2.i – Public health – DPA 2018, Schedule 1, Part 1, paragraph 3 9.2.j – Research – DPA 2018, Schedule 1, Part 1, paragraph 4 Law enforcement processing Processing personal data for law enforcement purposes is covered by Part 3 of the DPA 2018.
There are different conditions that apply.
Where processing is taking place for law enforcement, you need to check whether you are listed as a competent authority in Schedule 7 of the DPA If you are not listed in Schedule 7, you may still be a competent authority if you have a legal power to process personal data for law enforcement purposes.
For example, local authorities who prosecute trading standards offences or the Environment Agency when prosecuting environmental offences.
A key question regarding processing for law enforcement purposes is whether law enforcement is the primary purpose for processing the data shared between the parties.
In terms of safeguarding children, where data is shared for ensuring their safety and wellbeing, it is likely that law enforcement is not the primary purpose of a local authority.
However, it may be the purpose for a police force, in the same Data Sharing Agreement, for the prevention and detection of crime.
For example, data shared by the local authority regarding the situation around a child may indicate criminality on behalf of one or more parents, which the police would then need to investigate.
Local authorities may be processing for both usual purposes and law enforcement purposes, for example when a Youth Offending Team is involved.
It is possible that law enforcement processing may fall outside the scope of the Data Sharing Agreement.
If the data has been shared for the primary purpose of safeguarding but further processing is necessary for law enforcement by the police, then the police are responsible for ensuring that activity is done in a compliant manner.
For more guidance see the ICO Guidance on Law Enforcement processing link in the guidance for this section.

Safeguarding of children and individuals at risk) DPA 18, Schedule 1, Part 3 - Additional conditions relating to criminal convictions etc: n/a Police: DPA 18, Schedule 1, Part 1 – Conditions relating to employment, health and research etc: n/a DPA 18, Schedule 1, Part 2 – Substantial public interest conditions: n/a DPA 18, Schedule 1, Part 3 - Additional conditions relating to criminal convictions etc: n/a The sharing is for one of the law enforcement purposes – defined as the purposes of the prevention, investigation, detection or prosecution of criminal offences or the execution of criminal penalties, including the safeguarding against and the prevention of threats to public security – the sharing falls under the scope of Part 3 of the Data Protection Act 2018 (DPA) with the police acting as a competent authority.

It is therefore necessary for the police to be able to understand if an individual is open to specific services and for the police to then share information with that professional.
For disclosure to the police by the local authority, the local authority relies on Article 9(2)(g) of the UK GDPR.

Lawfulness – Data Protection Act 2018 – what your DPO will need to know It is likely that the lawful basis for processing of special category data for safeguarding reasons is under the basis of Article 9(2)(g), substantial public interest of the UK GDPR.
This will require organisations to meet additional conditions and safeguards set out in UK law, in Schedule 1 of the DPA 2018.
All relevant partner organisations must determine the relevant condition for processing before they begin sharing/processing the data.
It is an additional requirement to have an appropriate policy document in place in order to meet some of the Schedule 1 conditions.
This Data Sharing Agreement might be sufficient to function as the appropriate policy document as it is likely that all relevant aspects are covered within it.

Non-interference – common law duty of confidentiality How to complete There are three general approaches to sharing personal data without interference with the common law duty of confidentiality.
These are if you have consent from the individual (data subject), if there is a substantial public interest which allows you to process the information in question or if there is a legal duty (e.g., a court order in place asking you to disclose information or clear duty to share in legislation).
You should utilise the most appropriate condition for the circumstances.
It is of note that consent under the Common Law Duty of Confidentiality is not the same then consent as a lawful basis under data protection law.
Consent can be implied and is a valid basis under the common law duty of confidentiality (in contrary to consent under data protection law which must be freely given, specific, and involve an affirmative action (UK GDPR Article 7 compliance)).
This can be achieved by the individual(s) being made aware (informed) at which point they can raise queries or concerns if they have any.
The conditions to be met for the common law duty of confidentiality are different to the conditions for processing under UK GDPR.
However, you can consider them in a similar way, and use the GDPR conditions to describe why the common law duty is met.
Local authorities and their sharing partners will very likely share information with each other on the basis of public interest for safeguarding children.
This includes the protection of individuals from neglect or physical, mental, or emotional harm but also the protection of physical, mental or emotional well-being of an individual.
This doesn’t mean individuals should not be informed and engaged about the sharing of their data, but that they should understand why it needs to be done.
The best approach in general in safeguarding (or potential) circumstances is to consider sharing on the basis of substantial public interests and when doing so inform the relevant individual(s) about what, why and who, unless the circumstances are such that to inform could increase the risk to individual(s).
Please state here and explain how you will be satisfying Confidentiality: Consent: n/a Substantial public interest: Sharing initiative is based on the public interest to Safeguard children and individuals at risk.

Non-interference – common law duty of confidentiality – example scenarios Scenario 1: A local authority children’s social care department is sharing safeguarding relevant information with a MultiAgency Safeguarding team in order to allow for a risk assessment of specific safeguarding concerns to be completed to allow to make an informed decision on what to do to best protect a vulnerable child and family part of the case.
The circumstances describe a scenario of non-interference with the common law duty of confidentiality because sharing is done in reliance with the public interest condition under the UK GDPR and DPA18.
Scenario 2: A local authority receives a court order stating that all information held about a child known to the authority must be disclosed within two weeks’ time in order to inform decision making at court.
This includes all relevant and highly sensitive information which can be classed as safeguarding relevant.
The individuals records include details of child sexual exploitation, self-harm and neglect by parents and carers of the individual.
Disclosure of information is required by law.
The duty of confidentiality is overridden and compliance with the court order instructions is required.
Scenario 3: Social worker asks parent if they would like to attend a parenting course.
Parent says yes.
The social worker tells them who runs the service and that they will be sending over relevant information about their circumstances to help them arrange an appointment and ensure they are put on the right course.
The social worker sends a follow up letter to confirm this with a link to further information about the use of their information.
So, they’ve agreed to attend the parenting course and been informed about the use of their data as part of this, and they have not raised any objections to the sharing of their data.
This therefore satisfies the common law duty of confidentiality as there is implied consent on this basis.
Non-interference – common law duty of confidentiality – what your DPO will need to know To determine/confirm whether the intended sharing satisfies the common law duty of confidentiality, the DPO will need to understand what is being shared (i.e. is it subject to the common law duty? ), why it is being shared (i.e. the grounds/purpose for sharing) and will the individuals to whom it pertains be informed of the sharing.
The DPO will also look at the elements of transparency (see section 8) and subject rights (see section 9).
