Non-interference – Human Rights Act 1998, Article 8 How to complete The Human Rights Act 1998, Article 8 (HRA) sets out the fundamental rights and freedoms that everyone in the UK is entitled to (e.g. the right to marry or the right to be protected from discrimination).
It gives public authorities a legal framework to help them to assure that everything they do respects the human rights of the individuals they are providing services for.
Article 8 is the right to respect for private and family life (privacy) and is relevant when considering information sharing (are we assured of noninterference with everyone’s right to respect for private and family life, their home and their correspondence? ).
The right of respect for private and family life may be restricted.
If so, please state why this is necessary and if it is proportionate (e.g. necessary if balanced against the protection of the rights and freedoms of others, not more than required to achieve the purpose for sharing).
In practice the right to respect for private and family life is very similar to the common law duty of confidentiality and the same general bases that support data sharing under the common law will support interference with the right to privacy.
Article 8 states: There shall be no interference by a public authority with the exercise of this right except such as is in accordance with the law and is necessary in a democratic society in the interests of national security, public safety or the economic wellbeing of the country, for the prevention of disorder or crime, for the protection of health or morals, or for the protection of the rights and freedoms of others.
There are clear links in safeguarding circumstances with the protection of health, the protection of rights (e.g. right to life, prohibition of torture) and in some cases the prevention of crime.

Non-interference – Human Rights Act 1998, Article 8 – what your DPO will need to know If you disclose or share personal data only in compliance with the common law duty of confidentiality and the current UK Data Protection legislation (UK GDPR & DPA 18) it is likely that you will also meet the requirements under and therefore comply with Article 8 of the HRA.

Transparency How to complete There are a number of things to consider when managing transparency to ensure individuals are informed about how their data is being processed, why it is being processed and what rights are available to them in order to have control over the process of sharing/processing.
Considerations and expectations are as follows: Provide Privacy Notice content including the required information under Article 13 and 14 of the UK GDPR Provide the information in a timely manner as per Article 13 and 14 of the UK GDPR Assure that privacy information is provided in an effective manner for the target audience Are your staff aware of their obligations around transparency and how the organisation expects privacy information to be provided?
Please consider any relevant exemptions from the duty to provide privacy information.
For example, where informing a data subject may impact the ability to investigate crime, or where it may risk serious harm to the physical or mental health of any individual.

Scenario A local authority went live with the nationwide Child Protection – Information Sharing project (CP-IS) recently.
It requires the local authority to upload details about all looked after children or children subject to a child protection plan.
The information can then be shared with clinical staff in unscheduled healthcare settings to help them make more informed decisions.
At the same time, CP-IS notifies the local authority if and when a child presents for unscheduled treatment anywhere in England.
In order to comply with transparency under Article 5, 12, 13 and 14 of the UK GDPR the local authority updated their current privacy information on the public facing website to include the above information (as correspondence and service materials link to the website for privacy information).
The local authority also got their communications team and patient advocates/ representatives to ensure the content is provided as per UK GDPR requirements above (e.g. clear plain language).
Transparency – what your DPO will need to know Consider that some individuals (e.g. children, individuals with cognitive issues or learning difficulties, individuals with English as a second language) need particular protection when processing their personal data to assure they understand any potential risks and are fully protected.
Privacy Notices should therefore be written in a simple and clear way to assure they understand why their data is being shared/processed, what will happen with it and what their rights are.
It should be considered if separate privacy information should be made available.
Additionally the effectiveness of the existing privacy information should be assessed.
Are there proactive tools to inform individuals, is a combination of different tools being used, is it written in a way that is understood by the target audience.
An emphasis should also be put on automated decisionmaking and profiling.
Can individuals access the data for review and accuracy assurance.
Are individuals aware of what the impact could be and do they understand the process of using the data.
Are they aware of the rights they have and how to exercise them.

Individual rights How to complete Every individual is entitled to have their personal information protected, used in a fair and lawful way, and made available to them when they ask for a copy.
If an individual feels that their personal information is factually incorrect they are entitled to ask for that information to be corrected.
The responsibility to comply with individual rights requests and therefore to establish how they are managed lawfully lays with the controllers of the information being shared/ processed and must be taken seriously.
Processes must be agreed with all controllers (if more than one) to allow individuals to exercise their rights in a straight forward and safe way.
Emphasis must be put on managing requests considering exemptions (e.g., disclosure of third party information or information which could cause severe harm and distress); following legal requirements (e.g. legal timeframes, providing regulator contact details); and allowing case by case assessments involving the relevant parties, but at the same time making it easy and understandable for individuals to exercise their rights.
Sharing partners may be able to specifically state an agreed process for how to manage individual rights (including subject access request) if agreed in advance.
Processes documentation (e.g. process map, standard operating procedures (SOPs)) can be added to the Data Sharing Agreement as an appendix.
In terms of safeguarding children, any processes must be set out with the safeguarding of the child at the centre.
Requests to exercise data protection rights may come from children, or often someone with parental responsibility.
Consideration must be given to the age and capacity of the child when the request comes from someone with parental responsibility.
The Data Sharing Agreement must link to sufficient partner organisational policy and process to deal with such requests and detail how these are tackled in a collaborative manner where data is shared.
NB where the example refers to ‘system’ that can be taken to mean a shared database either set up specifically or where partners provide access to each other’s systems.
State below what processes relevant partner organisations have in place to enable data subjects to exercise their information rights: The right of access: Any controller subject to this Data Sharing Agreement could receive a subject access request (SAR) for shared data processed/held on an individual in their own system or a shared one.
When such a request is received then the receiving party will be the co-ordinating party for the response and will contact the other relevant parties and inform them the request has been received.
As the frameworks applied to SARs are slightly different between all parties (in terms of exemptions and requirements to inform), then each partner will check their data in the system and determine what can be disclosed.
The co-ordinating party will require the other parties to provide their disclosable data by an agreed date, so that the sum of disclosable information from the data base can be provided to the data subject within the appropriate legal timeframe.
The right of rectification: Any identified requirement for rectification received should be directed to the source system/organisation that the data comes from immediately.
Outcomes will be shared with all relevant parties as and if required and actions will be put in place accordingly.
The right to restrict processing: Any identified requirement for the restriction of processing received should be directed to the source system/organisation that the data comes from immediately.
Outcomes will be shared with all relevant parties as and if required and actions will be put in place accordingly.
State below what processes relevant partner organisations have in place to enable data subjects to exercise their information rights: The right to object: Any objection received to the processing of data related to the sharing covered in this agreement needs to be carefully considered.
If the receiving organisation is not best placed to respond they should direct the requestor (or pass with requestor’s permission) to the relevant organisation.
The organisation should make a determination based on the reasons for the objection and whether there are any compelling legitimate reasons on which they could refuse.
It is quite possible many safeguarding situations are such that there would be compelling legitimate basis to refused an objection.
However each case must be judged on its merits and determined individually.
Rights in relation to automated decision making and profiling: Some of the activities within the use of the database are calculating items (e.g. vulnerability/risk scores), this is however not solely automated decision making or profiling as there will always be human intervention before a decision will be made, therefore at present this right does not apply.
This will be kept under review as the use of the data and the system output products develop.
The right to be informed is covered under 8 Transparency of this DSA: Processing for reasons of safeguarding in this case will be done under the ‘public task’ basis.
The following rights would not apply in this example: Right to erasure Right to portability Right to object (applies for public task but not for legal obligation)
Individual rights – example scenarios Scenario 1: The police is sharing relevant information with the local authority under the Supporting Families Programme to allow early intervention and prevention around risks of child sexual exploitation and NEET (Not in Education, Employment or Training).
The local authority onward shares some of the information to educational settings within the relevant area in order for schools to provide children and young people with the best outcome possible and safeguard individuals as required.
Sharing partners have agreed for all individual rights requests for the relevant information to be directed to the local authority and for the police to be involved in decision making around disclosures.
This has been documented within the Data Sharing Agreement and a Standard Operating Procedure and Process has been shared with all partners.
Scenario 2: The local authority is onboarded to the local Shared Care Record and can access relevant information from a number of local health care partners including GP’s, ambulance Services, the local hospital and mental health services.
It also provides relevant local authority data around vulnerabilities to the Shared Care Record.
The Shared Care Record Programme has written a Data Subject’s Right Policy which has been signed off by the IG Group and Programme board.
The policy describes in detail how the programme and it’s sharing partners will uphold those rights.
All relevant partners have access to the policy to help ensure that staff are informed and well equipped to support individuals exercising their rights.
The policy works in conjunction with and does not replace the local authority’s policy in relation to upholding individuals rights.
Individual rights – what your DPO will need to know Individual Rights are established under chapter III – Rights of the data subject, UK GDPR.
Your DPO must be assured that compliance is managed.
Checks need to be completed to assure that relevant policies and procedures are in place to manage individual rights.
It must be documented what processes have been agreed and how responsibilities have been divided between partners (e.g. which organisation produces the privacy notice, handles data subject access requests etc. ).
All relevant staff must be aware of those policies and procedures in order to allow them to follow the required process once requests are being received.
Relevant staff also must be trained to understand the legal requirements for responding to individuals right requests (e.g. legal timeframes, ways of how they can be received, what rights are relevant).
Requests can come into the organisation in different ways and can be directed at any staff member.
Individual Rights for law enforcement processing are established under Part 3, Chapter 3 of the DPA18.

How data sharing will be carried out – example scenarios Scenario 1: A shared care record application is developed to enable partnership working.
The application is developed by a third party organisation (‘supplier’) led by the local authority who own the application/asset.
It is agreed that multiple organisations will share key, relevant data into the shared record to enable more effective partnership working.
The data will be used for the provision of care to individuals so needs to be reasonably up-to-date to reduce need for additional contacts by other means (i.e. telephone calls and/or emails).
As such, the organisations involved share the key, relevant data via encrypted transfer mechanisms (overseen by the system supplier), sharing updates/changes to the previous data feed (to reduce amount of data transferred and processing load).
Detail of the various data sources, the technical methods of transfer and uploading into the application are held in documents managed by the local authority overseeing the development, implementation and maintenance of the application.
Risks and mitigations for the methods of transfer and upload are assessed and addressed within the Data Protection Impact Assessment for the programme.
Scenario 2: A group of public sector organisations from across health, social care, education and the police have established a monthly ‘data sharing’ meeting and have a set of criteria they use to identify individuals on their separate caseloads that may benefit from a multi-disciplinary discussion to ensure these individuals are offered and receiving appropriate support.
Prior to each meeting the staff attending have a report that they run on their organisational systems to highlight the particular individuals and provide a summary of data on each.
This is sometimes complemented by staff reviewing the individuals’ records and noting other key information.
This is then shared verbally at the meeting and a record of the discussions and actions related to each individual is made.
This is stored in a shared electronic space that each service can access.
The shared space has been provided by the local authority who are responsible for the security of the shared space and providing access to the relevant staff from each partner.
The partner agencies are responsible for identifying specific staff who should have access.
How data sharing will be carried out – what your DPO will need to know The DPO needs to know the procedures for the transfer of data, to help assess risks to the data and necessary mitigations.
This is relevant to the specific data sharing agreement, and helps the DPO ensure that your organisation’s processes comply with external standards for data security, such as that needed for access to the government’s Public Services Network (PSN) or the Data Security & Protection Toolkit (DSPT) required for access to NHS systems.
For manual/procedural sharing: Identification of data sources and flows and agreed methods for transfer (manual, email, phone call etc).
For sharing that is supported with technical solutions/ applications: What are the transfer options to enable the objectives of the sharing to be met?
Has the organisation’s IT Security Manager or similar role approved the IT security standards?
Are there written procedures for how data will be transferred?
How will staff know about these procedures?
Do you need to provide external guidance, such as how an individual can use the council’s secure email system/ portal such as Egress or Encrypt & Send.
See section 11 for information on whether any personal data is shared or accessible outside of the UK.

Abbreviations and glossary Ad-hoc data sharing Information sharing outside a formal meeting or system, often on a one-off basis.
Appropriate Policy Document (APD) An appropriate policy document is a short document outlining your compliance measures and retention policies.
It is required under the Data Protection Act 2018 for some of the conditions documented in Schedule 1 (Part 1, 2 and 3).
Caldicott Guardian A senior person responsible for protecting the confidentiality of people’s health and care information and making sure it is used properly.
All NHS organisations and local authorities which provide social services must have a Caldicott Guardian.
Further, guidance has been issued under the Health and Social Care (National Data Guardian) Act 2018 that recommends “other organisations providing services as part of the publicly funded health service, adult social care, or adult carer support” should have a Caldicott Guardian by 30/06/2023: Caldicott_Guardian_guidance_v1.0_27.08.21.pdf Commissioning Support Unit (CSU) CSUs are organisations whose primary purpose is to provide Integrated Care Boards with external support, specialist skills and knowledge to support them in their role as commissioners.
They were established following the changes brought about by the Health and Social Care Act 2012, to support Clinical Commissioning Groups (now ICBs) after Primary Care Trusts were retired.
However, CSUs have evolved to provide a much wider array of services, with a broad portfolio, such as supporting national programmes and providers of all types.
Common law duty of confidentiality The common law duty of confidentiality is not codified; it is based on previous judgements in court.
Whilst various interpretations of the common law may be possible it is widely accepted that, where information which identifies individual service users is provided and held in confidence, disclosure may only be justified in one of three ways: the service user has given consent for their information to be used; the balance of public and private interest favours public interest disclosure; or a statutory basis exists which permits or requires disclosure.
(source: Health and Social Care (Control of Data Processing) Act (Northern Ireland) 2016, Explanatory Note, Common Law Duty of Confidentiality)

Data Controller / Joint Controller The natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body which, alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes and means of the processing of personal data.
Data Protection Act (DPA) 2018 The DPA 2018 sits alongside and supplements the UK Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) A process to help you identify and minimise the data protection risks related to processing of personal data.
A DPIA is legally required in some circumstances.
Data Protection Officer (DPO) The primary role of the data protection officer (DPO) is to ensure that their organisation processes the personal data of its staff, customers, providers or any other individuals (also referred to as data subjects) in compliance with the applicable data protection rules.
Data Subject The individual to whom the data being processed relates and is identified/identifiable by that data.
Data Sharing Data sharing as used within this document can be understood as sharing of personal data.
Data Sharing Agreement (DSA) Terminology can vary (Data Sharing Protocol, Data Sharing Contract, Personal Data Sharing Agreement), but can be used interchangeably in guidance.
A DSA can be used between sharing partners (Controllers) to help demonstrate compliance with the UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR), the Data Protection Act 2018, the common law duty of confidentiality and other relevant laws.
It should help you justify your data sharing, clarify responsibilities of the sharing partners and set agreed parameters for the use of data.

Legal gateway Legislation and common law that establishes justifiable grounds for the processing of personal data.
Local Authority (LA) An LA is a local government organisation responsible for the administration of government policy at a local level.
Means [of processing] Actions taken in the processing of data to achieve the purpose(s) for its processing i.e. how the data is processed but can also be considered to extend to what data is used to achieve the purpose(s).
Modelling The application of structured analysis, or use, of data.
Multi-Agency Safeguarding Hub (MASH) The Multi-Agency Safeguarding Hub (MASH) brings key professionals together to facilitate early, better quality information sharing, analysis, and decision-making, to safeguard vulnerable children and young people more effectively.
Personal data Data that relates to a living identified or identifiable individual.
Processor A natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body which processes personal data on behalf of the controller.
Purpose(s) [of processing] Reasons to process personal data.
Risk Scoring The application of a value/score based on a set of relevant risk factors and calculations/algorithms Role-based access control (RBAC) A model for controlling access to resources (i.e., data) where permitted actions on resources are identified with roles.
(e.g., an employee with a health/care professional role may access full service user health/care records, whilst a health/care service administrator may only access limited details from service user health/care records).
Secure File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) A protocol for securely accessing and transferring large files across the web.
Senior Information Risk Owner (SIRO) The SIRO is responsible for managing information risks.
In small organisations, this might be part of a combined role.
If the organisation appoints an IG Lead who is not part of the senior management team or board, then there should be a SIRO who they report to at the highest level of the organisation.
Organisations operating under the standard NHS contract are required to assign the role of SIRO.
Special Category Data Data pertaining to an identified or identifiable individual that reveals their racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, or trade union membership, and the processing of genetic data, biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person, data concerning health or data concerning a natural person’s sex life or sexual orientation.
Supporting Families Supporting Families is part of a national programme that helps thousands of families across England to get the help they need to address multiple disadvantages through a whole-family approach, delivered by keyworkers, working for local authorities and their partners.
UK Data Protection Legislation For the purpose of this template/guidance the UK data protection legislation means the UK GDPR and the DPA 2018 and regulations made under the DPA 2018 which apply to a party relating to the use of personal data.

Toolkit 1: Informal sharing ‘Informal’ sharing refers to sharing that needs to take place between professionals that isn’t via a shared system/database or via a formal committee (e.g. MDT meeting, MASH etc).
Informal sharing may well lead onto more formalised actions or may come from procedural sharing via a system or database.
In essence this relates to the ‘corridor conversation’ between a nurse and a social worker, or police officer etc.
When faced with an opportunity to ask or tell.
You may well find yourself with the opportunity to ask or tell a colleague (internal or external) for information on a child(ren) and family you are involved with.
In this situation consider: Would the child(ren)/family reasonably expect you to speak to your colleague about them?
If they may not reasonably expect you to do so, but you feel the colleague is likely to be able to help you ensure their wellbeing or their safety, or you need to tell them something to assist with their involvement, then you should have the conversation with your colleague.
When seeking an opportunity to ask or tell.
This is similar to the above, but when the conversation is more planned, i.e, deciding to call or email a contact.
The only difference is that if you are unsure about whether the child(ren)/family would reasonably expect you to have the conversation and you can’t easily justify having the conversation without their knowledge, then there is the opportunity to have a discussion with them first, if that is appropriate.
This isn’t to get their consent but to ensure they are informed.
If the circumstances are urgent and delay may increase the risk in a safeguarding context or in fact discussion with the family may also increase the risk, then that is a robust basis to have the conversation without involvement of the child(ren)/family.
When asked about something you know.
As with the above circumstances this may be an unplanned conversation or one you’ve scheduled to have.
The same approach will generally apply, when you are asked, consider if the child(ren)/family would reasonably expect you to answer or if the circumstances of the case warrant and urgent response or if seeking family involvement would potentially increase risk to the child(ren).
Having a conversation, not a question and answer session.
Sharing information is critical to effective safeguarding.
Many agencies involved can be said to have a ‘need to know’.
However, if the sharing is simply a question and answer session, then key information may not get shared.
If you decide that the requestor needs to know the answer you can give them, also think around the wider context of what you know, that they may need to be told, which may be things they haven’t asked for as they don’t know what you know.
Checklist of things to consider: Do you need to identify who you are talking about?
Can you have a conversation along the lines of ‘I have a case of ‘x’ where ‘y’ might be taking place, what would you advise I do about it?’.
Often you will need to discuss specific individuals, but before you do consider if you can discuss anonymously first?
Inform the individual before sharing where appropriate and where it does not prevent sharing that is urgent to ensure the safeguarding of an individual.
How much do you need to share?
It is important to remember data sharing should be kept to the minimum necessary, but the minimum could be quite a lot.
Also of note is that the relevant legal principle starts by stating ‘adequate, relevant’ before mentioning limits.
When sharing consider the confidence you have in the accuracy of data, highlighting any concerns you may have.
Do discuss whether data can be shared beyond the conversation you are having, so others are aware of your views on that aspect.
Document the sharing as soon as possible, by making appropriate notes about what you’ve shared and why and also what you have been told (this may be a note on a file, or logging a disclosure request).
Toolkit 2: Levels of identifiability Article 5 (c) of UK GDPR requires that personal data shall be ‘adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (‘data minimisation’)’.
You must only use the minimum amount of personal data necessary to achieve the stated purpose, and controllers must describe why they need the specified data.
The purpose may be achieved using pseudonymised or anonymised data.
Reducing the level of identifying factors in any data to the minimum required reduces the risk to privacy and the likelihood of a damaging impact if mistakes are made with the data.
For example, if a dataset contains a social care reference number for each person and details of their social care needs, but no detail on their name, specific address or other identifiers, then if the dataset is sent to the wrong person, the likelihood of damage or distress being caused is reduced.
Controllers must consider whether individuals may still be identifiable by others, even where it is not required nor justified in respect of the purpose for processing.
Despite steps to pseudonymise/anonymise data, the context of the data, i.e. a combination of information and/or low numbers of individuals, means that identification of individuals is possible.
You should take further steps to mitigate the risk of identification, such as restricting access to processing outputs or suppressing data with low numbers.
Personal data Data that can be used to identify an individual, such as: Name Date of birth NHS number Home address National Insurance number Employee reference number Pseudonymised data Pseudonymisation refers to techniques that replace, remove or transform information that identifies individuals, and keep that information separate.
The data is changed so that the personal data can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information, provided that such additional information is kept separately and is subject to technical and organisational measures to ensure that the personal data are not attributed to an identified or identifiable natural person.
Techniques include replacing personal data with a unique reference that is restricted to only those that need to be able to identify the individual.
Pseudonymised data is still considered personal data under the UK GDPR.
Anonymised data UK GDPR (recital 26) defines anonymous data as: information which does not relate to an identified or identifiable natural person or to personal data rendered anonymous in such a manner that the data subject is not or no longer identifiable.
Effectively anonymised data There is a correlation between ‘effectively anonymised data’ and ‘pseudonymised data’.
However ‘effectively anonymised’ is a wider form of data.
In pseudonymised data, all or most of the identifiers have been removed and replaced with a pseudonym (often a reference number) that as few organisations and individuals as possible can reverse if needs be.
‘Effectively anonymised data’ is data that has had identifiers removed to the point that it is unlikely to be identifiable as risk of re-identification is sufficiently remote, taking account of the context, scope and purposes of what the data is used for, technical measures to protect the data, the environment in which the data is to be disclosed.
Identifiable in context Where it is not intended for individuals to be identified but it is possible to identify individuals from the data/ information included.
For example, it may be possible to identify an individual from a description or by something specific that they are quoted to have said that others would have heard them say.
It may be possible to identify someone through a combination of data, such as a postcode combined with equalities data like ethnicity, health condition or religion.
Low number suppression Individuals may be identified when data/information is attributed/linked and refers to a small number of individuals.
For example, the following data may clearly be linked to an individual if they are the only person of the characteristics living in a particular place: male, Chinese, prosthetic arm, living in postcode district XX11.
In such instances results are often suppressed and reported as “less than 5” or categories can be merged, age brackets increased, etc.
Further links and guidance Guidance on anonymisation and pseudonymisation ICO call for views: Anonymisation, pseudonymisation and privacy enhancing technologies guidance ICO
Toolkit 3: What is a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) (From the ICO’s guide to UK GDPR) You must do a DPIA for processing that is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals.
This includes some specified types of processing.
You can use screening checklists to help you decide when to do a DPIA.
It is also good practice to do a DPIA for any other major project which requires the processing of personal data.
Your DPIA must: describe the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing; assess necessity, proportionality and compliance measures; identify and assess risks to individuals; and identify any additional measures to mitigate those risks.
To assess the level of risk, you must consider both the likelihood and the severity of any impact on individuals.
High risk could result from either a high probability of some harm, or a lower possibility of serious harm.
Risk might be unnecessary intrusion into an individual’s privacy, or the potential for physical or mental harm if the data were used inappropriately.
You must consult your data protection officer (if you have one) and, where appropriate, individuals and relevant experts.
Any processors may also need to assist you.
If you identify a high risk that you cannot mitigate, you must consult the ICO before starting the processing.
Toolkit 4: Digital Economy Act 2017 From the ICO’s ‘Data sharing across the public sector: the Digital Economy Act codes’: Part 5 of the Digital Economy Act 2017 (DEA) focuses on digital government, providing gateways that allow specified public authorities to share data with each other.
Some of these gateways enable the sharing of personal data, while others allow the sharing of non-identifying data.
The objectives and purposes for data sharing under the DEA powers are tightly defined.
Under the DEA you must still comply with the data protection legislation.
Part 5 of the DEA explicitly: States that all processing of information under the DEA powers must comply with data protection legislation; and prohibits the disclosure of information where it would contravene data protection legislation.
“Examples of where the DEA may be used as a legal gateway for sharing data include: where the purpose is the improvement of the well-being of individuals or households (including physical, mental and emotional well-being of children).
Case example Somerset Council have registered an Data Sharing Agreement with the DEA as its legal gateway for the following purpose: Providing early intervention opportunities and presenting multi-agency data pertaining to social issues to a range of frontline professionals.
The integration and sharing of this joined up data will elicit a deeper and broader understanding of the multiple issues affecting individuals/ families.
It will reduce duplication and resource for practitioners supporting the family, as it contains headline detail on assessments and current and historic involvement, not just with statutory services, but commissioned providers.
It will: identify families facing multiple disadvantages enable the improvement or targeting of appropriate support to individuals or households enable the improvement of the physical, mental, emotional, social or economic wellbeing of individuals and families”
Toolkit 5: Consent considerations Consent under the UK General Data Protection Regulation is just one lawful basis for processing of personal data.
It is unlikely for you to require consent in data protection law to share data about a child, young person or family member if the sharing is for safeguarding reasons.
However, you do need a lawful basis in data protection legislation to share personal data, but consent is just one of the options available.
Instead, it is likely that, depending upon the type of organisation you are and the circumstances, the appropriate lawful bases will be public task, legitimate interests, legal obligation or vital interests.
The ICO’s interactive lawful basis guidance tool and guidance on Consent | ICO will help you to choose the right one.
When is consent inappropriate?
It follows that if for any reason you cannot offer people a genuine choice over how you use their data, consent will not be the appropriate basis for processing.
This may be the case if, for example: you would still process the data on a different lawful basis if consent were refused or withdrawn; you ask for ‘consent’ to the processing as a precondition of accessing your services; or you are in a position of power over the individual – for example, if you are a public authority or an employer processing employee data.
A common issue related to consent is the misunderstanding about consent under data protection law and consent in a different context, such as the provision of services by a local authority or the provision of healthcare by the NHS.
Consent to receive treatment or a service offered by an organisation or team is different from consent as a lawful basis under data protection law.
As stated earlier, it is unlikely to be appropriate to use consent as a lawful basis under data protection law; other lawful bases will be more suitable.
It is important to keep in mind that whichever lawful basis the processing of personal data is based on does not alter the requirement to inform individuals of how their data is being used (unless there is a legitimate reason not to inform them).

HISPC Interorganizational Agreements Collaborative Final Report G-1 USER GUIDE: PUBLIC HEALTH DATA SHARING AGREEMENT
User Guide HISPC Interorganizational Agreement (IOA) for Electronic Health Information Exchange Public Health-to-Public Health Data Sharing Agreement Developed by the Interorganizational Agreements Collaborative1 (IOA) of the Health Information Security and Privacy Collaboration (HISPC) Project March 2009 This User Guide is for parties using data sharing agreements to enter into electronic health information exchange (eHIE) efforts.
Two data sharing agreements for eHIE were developed as part of the HISPC Project.
This User Guide is a companion resource to the public-to-public data sharing agreement (Public Health Agreement) and explains the background, rationale, and other considerations related to use of the Public Health Agreement.
The IOA Collaborative and the HISPC Project are explained further in the document.
Background The IOA data sharing agreements (DSAs) are the result of several years of highly cooperative work among states, territories, and the federal government to resolve unnecessary barriers to interstate, interoperable, private, and secure eHIE.
When the Health Information Security and Privacy Collaboration (HISPC) was first established in 2006, 34 states,2 under the leadership of the prime contractor, RTI International, joined together to conduct a year-long project in which each participant would identify such barriers and propose implementation plans to address these impediments consistent with HIPAA,3 state privacy and security laws and regulations, and organizational policies.
In the next phase, the HISPC member states formed into groups to take steps to implement a specific project to resolve one of the barriers that had been identified in the earlier HISPC work.
Seven Collaboratives were formed under the supervision of the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC), one of which is the Interorganizational Agreements Collaborative (IOA).
Alaska, Guam, Iowa, North Carolina, New Jersey, and South Dakota4 are the members of IOA.
The Collaborative proposed to address the lack of available DSAs containing consistent privacy and security provisions to support cross-state electronic health information exchange (eHIE).
The third phase of the HISPC project resulted in two DSAs.
This User Guide addresses the Public Health Agreement.
A companion User Guide similarly addresses the Private Entity-toPrivate Entity Data Sharing Agreement.
Throughout all phases of the IOA work, the guiding principle has been mutually acceptable resolution of barriers consistent with applicable privacy and security laws and regulations.
The overall purpose was to create agreements that could be used throughout the country for standard arrangements that have received significant review and that are consistent among participants.
Mission The IOA-drafted DSAs can be used in the following situations: Public health agency-to-public health agency exchange of protected health information (PHI) that is held in public health registries pursuant to various federal and state laws.
Information specific to the Public Health Agreement begins with the “Guidelines for Completing the Public Health Agreement” section below.
Private entity-to-private entity exchange of PHI among private entities such as between hospitals, medical centers, regional health information organizations, laboratories, payors, PHRs, and other private organizations.
Information specific to private entity ePHI States shall mean states and territories.
HIPAA is the federal Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 and its implementing regulations on privacy and security, found at 45 C.F.R.
Two additional states participated in the process but ultimately were not able to continue to participate.
exchanges is found in the Private Entity-to-Private Entity Data Sharing Agreement User Guide, which is a companion to the Private-to-Private Data Sharing Agreement.
Development Steps The IOA developed a plan to ensure that the final work product would be suitable for use nationwide.
Thus, the IOA sought to create a national standard for use in specific types of circumstances, such as sharing public health registry information and provider-to-provider eHIE.
The plan of action included the following steps: Approximately 50 documents (memorandums of understanding, DSAs, etc. ) were gathered and cataloged by the IOA as source material.
Each document was carefully reviewed.
Each provision in each document was classified according to its provenance and subject matter.
Similar provisions from different agreements were then extracted, combined, and placed next to each other in a master document.
This process resulted in a matrix of more than 350 pages in which similar provisions from the source documents were grouped together for side-by-side comparison.
The provision categories included privacy, security, immunity, conflict of law, and numerous other topics.
This development and review process included coordination and cooperation with the Nationwide Health Information Network (NHIN) Data Use and Reciprocal Support Agreement (DURSA) Work Group.
The IOA then selected the most effective language and provisions with consideration of any conflicts in state law.
This work included review by state-specific legal Work Groups as well as the IOA Collaborative as a whole, which removed any provisions felt to be illegal or ill-advised under state law.
At the end of this process, the IOA met to draft final templates for public-to-public and private-to-private electronic data sharing.
The template documents were delivered to participating state governments and private entities for use in actual electronic data sharing pilot projects.
Lessons learned from the pilot project were documented, and agreements were edited or augmented based on the experience of the pilots.
Additional vetting and endorsements of the agreements were obtained from outside agencies, as noted in the final section of this document.
Policy Decisions and Guiding Principles The template agreements were drafted for use across all jurisdictions.
HIPAA compliance was a guiding principle as part of an overall concern for privacy and security in eHIE.
Agreements pertain to information requested only for the purposes of treatment, payment, health care operations, and, in the case of the public-to-public agreement, public health data.
Specific categories of sensitive data, such as HIV and mental health information, are subject to state law and are not specifically addressed in these agreements.
Each party would only share information that can be shared without additional specific protections.
Each party will operate under and comply with its own applicable state law.
Detailed provisions and technological specifications for user authentication, auditing, access, and authorization are not included in the templates.
They are left to attachments agreed to by all parties.
Each party’s applicable state law will govern disputes, and in the event that a dispute cannot be resolved, the parties will look to federal law and the growing body of federal common law.
Participation is voluntary and can be terminated at will.
The IOA elected not to include governance provisions, as such provisions would limit the generality of the documents.
Entering into these agreements does not change ownership of data.
Guidelines for Completing the Public Health Agreement The Public Health Agreement is provided as a template.
Further information needs to be inserted by parties to each agreement as follows: Effective date; Parties; Public health agency; State/territory; Public health system names (data registry names); Notice names and addresses; Signature information (name, title, date); and Attachments, as applicable, based on the parties’ chosen structure for exchange and addition of parties (confidentiality agreement, timely delivery of information, standards, technological, and security specifications, etc. ).
Additional Considerations for the Public Health Agreement The agreements will require additional attachments drafted by the users in the areas of technological specifications and timeliness of data exchange.
See Section 3.0a. and 0c.iii. of the Public Health-to-Public Health Data Sharing Agreement.
There are many public health exchange scenarios applicable to this agreement.
To date, the IOA states have successfully used this agreement for immunization registry exchange.
It is planned that this agreement will be expanded for additional uses in the future.
Based on the experience of the IOA states, it is recommended that certain parties be involved in the review of these agreements in the early stages of a data sharing project.
These organizations may include the state attorney general’s office, governor’s office, senior management of the Department of Public Health, registry program directors, technical staff, and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) officials in each state.
Endorsements and/or Review of the Public Health Agreement American Immunization Registry Association (AIRA) During HISPC Phase III, the IOA Collaborative approached AIRA for its review and comment on the Public Health Data Sharing Agreement since the document was being used in the Iowa/South Dakota/Guam/New Jersey pilot electronic data sharing of live immunization data between the four members.
The IOA Collaborative and AIRA had a number of very cordial calls and e-mails to discuss changes that AIRA suggested.
The changes converted the IOA Public Health Data Sharing Agreement from a model document used in a pilot demonstration into a document that could be used for ongoing, continuing work among two or more public health registries.
The suggested and accepted changes did not change the IOA Public Health Data Sharing Agreement in any substantive way.
The AIRA endorsement letter dated January 2009 stated that the IOA Public Health Agreement is “formally endorsed by AIRA for use by all states and public health agencies for the interoperable exchange of public health immunization data.” AIRA has loaded the updated version of the public health DSA to their website http://www.immregistries.org/ for download and use by their members.
Public Health Data Standards Consortium (PHDSC) The PHDSC, established in July 2003, is a nonprofit membership-based organization of federal, state, and local health agencies; professional associations; academia; public and private sector organizations; international members; and individuals.
PHDSC’s goal is to empower the health care and public health communities with health information technology (health IT) standards to improve individual and community health.
On February 18, 2009, the Board of Directors of the PHDSC approved the endorsement of the Public Health Data Sharing Agreement model document that had been developed and tested during the HISPC Phase III project.
They stated that the availability of this model agreement will greatly simplify the establishment of much-needed health information exchanges between public agencies across state lines, such as the sharing of immunization information between states from immunization registries.
They look forward to working with the IOA Collaborative to advance the adoption and use of this agreement.
The PHDSC stated as part of its endorsement in February 2009 that “the availability of this model agreement will greatly simplify the establishment of much-needed health information exchanges between public agencies across state lines.” Kansas In the fall of 2008, the State of Kansas approached the IOA Collaborative asking if it could review the Public Health Data Sharing Agreement.
The IOA Collaborative agreed, and Kansas offered the following comments to the IOA Collaborative.
Kansas felt that the Data Sharing Agreement is too formal for sharing within Kansas “for the purposes of sharing data . . . among agencies . . . to support our Community Health Record pilot project to get immunization and lead screening data” as the state has “good pre-existing relationships and data sharing agreements in place for related projects.” Kansas did state that when the state does “embark on a statewide electronic record initiative in the future” that the IOA document will assist them.
Kansas will use the provisions within the Public Health Data Sharing Agreement as a foundation tool when it takes this important statewide step.
IOA Collaborative Public Health Pilot Iowa, South Dakota, Guam, and New Jersey signed the Public Health Data Sharing Agreement.
The pilot-testing phase began after the model agreements were finalized halfway through the HISPC Phase III contract period.
Pilot HIE project applications involved two or more states.
The multistate HIE pilot projects included: Iowa and South Dakota conducted a public health-to-public health Immunization Registry Exchange Project.
This pilot project exchanged the immunization registry data of those individuals 0–25 years of age who received treatment in bordering Iowa and South Dakota counties.
Iowa, South Dakota, Guam, and New Jersey conducted a four-way public health-topublic health Immunization Registry Exchange Project.
This pilot project exchanged the immunization registry data of individuals born in 1990.
This population represents a geographically mobile group of 18-year-olds that includes both college- and military-bound individuals.
New Jersey undertook several initiatives to promote and advance the mission of the IOA Collaborative and to expand the acceptance and use of the IOA Public Health Data Sharing Agreements.
These activities included: Meetings with New York State and City health IT officials to establish interstate exchanges of Immunization Registry data.
Meetings with the City of Philadelphia Department of Health and CDC officials to promote interstate exchange of Public Health Registry data.
Developed contacts with the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania Health Department for support in the New Jersey-Philadelphia immunization data exchange and for future data sharing opportunities with New Jersey.
Presentations to HIMSS, NGA, PAeHI and SLHIE on Public Health Data Sharing Agreements and the ability to share public health information data.
IOA representatives participated in two PA e-Health Initiative All-Committee Meetings and promoted HISPC initiatives to the group.
A director from the committee attended the HISPC National Conference in Bethesda, MD, in March
Integration of DSAs into New Jersey’s Electronic Medical Record exchange pilot project.
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) HISPC Interorganizational Agreements (IOA) Collaborative Model Data Sharing Agreements (DSAs) Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) What is HISPC?
Established in June 2006 by RTI International through a contract with the U.S.
Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), the Health Information Security and Privacy Collaboration (HISPC) originally comprised 34 states and territories.
Phase III of HISPC began in April 2008, comprising 42 states and territories, and aimed to address the privacy and security variations and challenges presented by electronic health information exchange (eHIE) through multistate collaboration.
What is the HISPC-IOA?
In HISPC Phase III, participants were split into seven privacy and security topics for collaborative work, one of which was the IOA Collaborative.
The IOA Collaborative included representatives from Alaska, Guam, Iowa, New Jersey, North Carolina, and South Dakota.
Early phases of HISPC recognized that efforts to draft eHIE agreements and legal language can be time consuming and inefficient and often present barriers to eHIE.
As a result, the IOA Collaborative proposed to develop and pilot test model DSAs.
The stated objectives were to: Develop a standardized set of model DSAs for eHIE focused on privacy and security; and Test use of the model agreements in actual data-sharing pilot projects across state lines.
The IOA Collaborative limited the scope of the project to two types of DSAs: Public health data exchange (“public-to-public” agreement); and Private entity data exchange (“private-to-private” agreement).
What is the mission of the HISPC-IOA?
The mission of the HISPC-IOA is to improve patient care and safety by developing and implementing model DSAs to facilitate inter- and intrastate eHIE.
The project outcome is a set of model DSAs and related tools that can be shared nationally and replicated to advance eHIE efforts.
What was the general process used by the HISPC-IOA Collaborative?
Through the use of HISPC-IOA legal Work Groups, the members of this collaborative reviewed a wide variety of memoranda of understandings, DSAs, and federal and state laws and regulations to develop consensus on core content and language.
The Collaborative also coordinated with key groups, such as the Nationwide Health Information Network (NHIN) Data Use and Reciprocal Support Agreement (DURSA) Work Group and the other HISPC multistate collaboratives, to ensure consistency and continuity of effort.
The IOA Collaborative documented a core set of privacy and security provisions and pilot tested the two model DSAs in real-life settings.
Lessons learned from the pilots were used to create Implementation User Guides.
Lastly, the IOA Collaborative requested additional review and feedback of the DSAs from various external organizations and agencies.
What are the primary product(s) of the IOA Collaborative work?
Two model DSAs: one for the public health setting and one for the private entity setting Core privacy and security contract provisions Implementation User Guides for the model DSAs Library of sample DSAs Compare/contrast analysis of the IOA model DSAs to the NHIN DURSA Pilot evaluation results and formal approval/endorsements of the IOA model DSAs Why should my organization use the HISPC-IOA model DSA(s)?
The IOA Collaborative developed products for replication by other states and organizations to avoid duplication of effort.
The IOA Collaborative took on this challenge so that organizations interested in eHIE would not have to go through a similar process and begin from scratch.
We expect others to benefit from having access to standardized, endorsed DSAs that have been tested in real-life scenarios.
Public health agencies and private health care entities can have confidence that the privacy and security aspects of the DSAs were thoroughly reviewed and vetted by experts in the field.
Successes and barriers were documented to streamline future efforts.
By providing template DSAs that can be easily customized, the IOA Collaborative aimed to create momentum toward utilization of standardized documents throughout the country that will in turn encourage increased health information exchange.
How does one use the HISPC-IOA model DSAs?
An organization should review the IOA model DSA templates and the respective Implementation User Guides with legal, medical, technical, and administrative representatives.
The DSA templates provide a core model legal document.
These templates can be modified, if necessary, through attachments to the core document to meet a specific organization’s legal, medical, and/or business needs.
My organization already has a DSA or memorandum of understanding (MOU) for such activities.
Why should my organization consider using the HISPC-IOA models?
The HISPC-IOA is not advocating changes to current legal agreements that are already in place and used successfully to support eHIE.
The HISPC-IOA model DSAs should be considered for new eHIE projects that will require new agreements or for existing agreements that need to be updated.
By using the HISPC-IOA model agreements, many hours of administrative and legal time will be saved.
Should IT technical details and/or specifications be included in the HISPC-IOA model DSA?
No. The HISPC-IOA model DSA templates are broadly worded to cover general areas of a DSA, with a special focus on privacy and security.
Project specifics, such as IT technical details, should be drafted and attached as an appendix to the core document that can be easily modified as the project evolves.
This accommodates the fact that technology changes more rapidly than the broader privacy and security provisions contained in the core document.
Appendices such as IT technical details should, however, support the basic privacy and security concepts in the HISPC-IOA core documents.
What information is contained the Implementation User Guide?
The Implementation User Guide is a companion resource for the model IOA DSAs that provides more explanation about the background, context, and use of the DSAs.
The guides include such topics as policy decisions and guiding principles and user considerations for completing the DSAs.
Have the HISPC-IOA DSAs been pilot tested in real-life settings?
If so, what organizations were involved in the pilots?
Once the model templates were established, the agreements were pilot tested to assess their application in real eHIE projects.
The pilot testing occurred in both the public health and private entity settings.
Actual immunization registry data was exchanged between Guam, South Dakota, Iowa, and New Jersey as part of the public health pilot project.
Preliminary approval of the agreements for future exchanges was obtained by 17 organizations in North Carolina and Alaska through the private pilot project.
Using both public and private entities helped validate and increase trust in the agreements for future data sharing projects.

No. The HISPC-IOA DSAs can be adapted for any form of health information exchange, including paper-based exchanges.
The same principles and high standards regarding the privacy and security of health care information should be applied to any mode of health information exchange.

This Data Sharing Agreement (the "Agreement") effective as of [insert date] (the "Effective Date") is between ALK-Abelló A/S, Bøge Allé 6-8, 2970 Hørsholm ("ALK") and [name of researcher], [address] (the "Researcher").
ALK and the Researcher are hereinafter also referred to individually as "Party" and collectively as "Parties".
ALK is committed to enhance public health through responsible sharing of clinical trial data.
The Researcher has requested access to certain clinical trial data for the purpose of conducting a research project.
ALK is willing to provide the Researcher with access to the clinical trial data under the terms and conditions set forth below.
The Researcher acknowledges that he/she will not be granted a direct access to the clinical data listed in Appendix A.
Instead ALK is willing to make the clinical data listed in Appendix A available to an independent statistician appointed by ALK (the "Consultant").
The Consultant will, at ALK's costs, perform the requested data analysis in accordance with the Researcher's statistical analysis plan provided by the Researcher to ALK (the analysis provided by the Consultant will hereinafter be referred to as the "Clinical Data").
The Parties will discuss and agree upon an overall timeline for the Consultant's work.
ALK is responsible for instructing the Consultant and the Researcher shall direct any requests and questions regarding the Consultant's work and the Clinical Data to ALK.
The Clinical Data will be provided to the Researcher by ALK upon the Consultant's completion of the analysis at no charge.
The Researcher acknowledges that the Clinical Data is provided as a service to the medical and scientific community and ALK bears no responsibility for the accuracy or content of the Clinical Data.
Subject to and conditional on the Researcher's compliance with this Agreement, ALK grants to the Researcher a limited, non-exclusive, royalty-free license to use the Clinical Data during the term of this Agreement solely to conduct the research specified in Appendix B (the "Research Project").
As between ALK and the Researcher, any title or ownership of the Clinical Data, including any intellectual property embodied therein, remains with ALK.
The Researcher may only use the Clinical Data: (i) for the purpose of the Research Project; (ii) in compliance with applicable laws, rules, regulations, codes of practise and ethical guidelines, including, but not limited to, all applicable laws and regulations relating to data protection and the privacy of subject health information; (iii) in compliance with ALK's policies and procedure for responsible clinical trial data sharing as stated on the following website: https://www.alk.net/rd/clinical-data-sharing; (iv) in accordance with the terms and conditions of this Agreement, additional restrictions set forth in Appendix A and ALK's written instructions; (v) in accordance with any regulatory and/or ethics approvals necessary to conduct the Research Project.
The Researcher shall obtain any such regulatory or ethics approvals and shall, upon ALK's request, provide a copy of such approvals to ALK.
The Researcher shall not: (i) use, or cause or permit the use of, the Clinical Data other than as expressly permitted under this Agreement; (ii) use, or cause or permit the use of, the Clinical Data or the results of the Research Project for any commercial purposes; (iii) transfer or distribute the Clinical Data to any third party without the prior written consent of ALK; (iv) use the Clinical Data in any manner that confers on any third party any proprietary rights in or to the Clinical Data, or that creates obligations to disclose the results generated or derived by the Researcher as the result of the Research Project under this Agreement to any third party (excluding disclosures pursuant to the publication provisions set forth in Clause 8); (v) seek to re-identify any individual, including without limitation, clinical trial participants and trial staff and/or combine the Clinical Data with other sources of data that would or could lead to the identification of any individual.
The Researcher shall maintain the Clinical Data in anonymized form.
The Researcher shall restrict access to and use of the Clinical Data to individuals as: (i) are directly engaged in performing the Research Project under the Researcher's direct control and supervision (specified in Appendix B) (the "Research Team"); (ii) need to access and use the Clinical Data for purposes of the Research Project; and (iii) have been informed of the access, use, transfer and disclosure restrictions of this Agreement and are subject to contractual obligations to comply with the same.
The Researcher shall be responsible for any violations of this Agreement by the members of the Research Team.

To Securely Erase data means to erase it in a manner that prevents it from being restored or reconstructed.
In the case of removable media such as tape or optical disk, this means destroying the media through shredding or physical destruction.
In the case of rewritable storage media such as disk, removable hard drive, thumb drive, solid state media or cloud storage media, the files must be overwritten with zeros or nulls and then deleted from the system.
Data Exchange means the transfer of data from a Data Owner to a Requester.
